title: The altitude finally got me
subtitle: Had to skip the Rainbow Mountains
content:
At 3,400 metres, plan 3–4 days of acclimation

I knew Cusco would be the highest city in Peru I’d be visiting and after spending a week in Arequipa at 2,300 metres, I thought I’d have gained a bit of acclimation credit but I was wrong.

I was surprised at how hard it was to breathe in the city and that I had a light headache the entire time so I bought some medication for the altitude after running out of what my doctor from home had prescribed.

I didn’t make any plans before starting the Salkantay hike four days after landing but I did want to sneak in a small hike at one of the rainbow mountains, Palccoyo. The hike itself was only about an hour and I really wanted to figure out my own transportation to explore at my will but the most affordable option was to join a small group tour.

I walked into the main square and explored breathlessly for a couple hours inquiring about the tour options. Most tours were being offered for 100–120 soles without entry included. There was an early stop for breakfast and one on the way back for lunch, both buffets at the same place and it would take around 3 hours to get to the mountain.

After realizing all of the available tours leave Cusco around 4 AM, I considered renting a car until my host mentioned it was probably dangerous to drive with all the unmarked speed bumps. I also wasn’t certain all the roads would be paved and remembered the most expensive vehicles are automatic, which is the only type of car I can drive. All of that plus gas made this unrealistic for me.

I didn’t love the idea of being in a van for 6 hours and only getting to hike for one but in any case, two days after arriving I paid for a tour to Palccoyo and set an alarm for 3:50 AM. I made sure to be asleep before 9 PM and had my bag packed beforehand.

I brought home vegan pad Thai for dinner after a delicious meal of mango ceviche and pumpkin cream earlier. I had started the day with avocado toast and chia pudding so my appetite seemed good.

It’s possible I ate too soon before going to bed and my new altitude medication had slowed my digestion because I woke up still very full and was extremely thirsty. Something about my body just felt off.

In the darkness, I dressed and brushed my teeth while waiting for my transportation. I popped more altitude medication and took something to prevent any nausea for the ride. In the 10 minutes I waited for the van to call, I listened to my body screaming at me not to do this.

I did not feel well enough to travel in a van full of people for fear of vomiting from the overstimulation and dinner I still felt was not digested. I probably wouldn’t have enjoyed the buffet food and really didn’t have the energy to be around strangers.

So I cancelled and when my phone rang, I told the organizer I was sick and wouldn’t be able to make it. Unfortunately that meant I wouldn’t be getting any money back but at that point nothing could come between me and another 8 hours of sleep.

I didn’t leave my accommodation until later the next day when I had to attend a briefing for the Salkantay trek and enjoyed continuing to order very affordable food delivery. My room didn’t have a kitchen and the home didn’t have a microwave but the host family allowed me to store my leftover Indian food in their fridge and heat it up on the stove the next day.

I kept experiencing long-lasting pins and needles in my feet and hands as a result of the altitude or the medication so I stopped taking it before my multi-day guided trek.

I wish I had more time to learn about and to explore Cusco. The narrow, stair-filled streets and alleyways lined with rainbow flags were so charming. There was a coffee festival happening in the main square and I would have loved to experience more local foods but there simply wasn’t time, given the need to acclimatize.

After the Salkantay trek and visit to Machu Picchu, I had one more night in Cusco that enabled me to visit a different area, high up many stairs closer to nature than where I had been originally.

The host recommended I take a short car ride from the centre but I elected to walk the 30 minutes, fully uphill. It was challenging with all my baggage but I relished the chance to see more of the city and the views looking back as I ascended each staircase were priceless.

Very close to where I was staying, there were open trails through a valley surrounded by mountains and I got to walk around the Temple of the Moon ruins. Locals were cuddled up on blankets sharing food and drink in private areas and it looked like a lovely place to hang out.

I didn’t walk for long because it looked like heavy rain was going to fall at any moment. I had taken an edible and was excited to organize my belongings for the next day’s flight, order delivery, shower and find local sweets for dessert.

Feelings check

I felt overwhelmed by the size and historical beauty of Cusco when I realized I wouldn’t have enough time or energy to walk around a significant part of it. The physical symptoms of the altitude were shocking to experience after having no issues in Huaraz or Arequipa, possibly thanks to my blood-thinning medication.

I had a very friendly welcome from my first host, her daughter and their puppy after arriving by Rappi from the airport. They walked me to a local pollería for a quarter chicken dinner with fries and helped me buy water for my time there before settling in.

Of course when I stepped out of the car, there were several neighbourhood dogs I knew would be a nuisance with their barking but thankfully I had become an expert in shoving plugs deep into my ear canals and blasting the white noise on my phone so I slept well.

Seeing all the rainbow flags was very reassuring in terms of what I assumed was proud LGBTQ+ acceptance but I later learned the flags are related to cultural pride and not gay pride so that was a bit disappointing.

I enjoyed the urban hike required to get to my second accommodation further into nature especially since I stopped experiencing altitude side effects. I loved the area I was staying in, away from the city and wished I had more than just one night there because there seemed to be many trails around!

My only issue occurred when I tried to order a Rappi to the airport on my final morning and no one would accept my request. I tried Uber, which was double the price, and a driver did accept but messaged me immediately to ask for more money because I was so far and Uber doesn’t pay enough. I agreed to give him the remaining cash I had on hand because I needed to book a car immediately but felt angry and exploited for the entire ride, wishing I gave myself more time to find something that matched the price the app was promoting. Uber gave me back what I paid in cash in Uber credits for my next ride and I know the money will go further for the driver and his family than it will for me but it still felt inappropriate.

where I stayed

Accommodation review: City

Large bedroom and living area on top floor of family home with ensuite & mountain view

Bed

Cozy queen-size with thick blankets to stay warm overnight and two perfectly contoured memory foam pillows.

Space

Artfully decorated open-concept space with bedroom, living and dining area containing smart TV, kettle and ensuite.

Views

Businesses across the street and homes rising up behind them to the top of a hill surrounded by flowers and greenery.

Neighbourhood

Filled with locals and dogs set 30 minutes by foot outside of the main square off a garden-lined alleyway near small shops.

Noise

Little to no noise from family in the home but barking dogs and fireworks throughout the day and overnight.

Host-pitality

Helpful and friendly hosts who greeted me upon arrival, gave me information about tours and checked in on my health.

Privacy

Felt removed from family and public being on the third floor but some windows required curtains to be closed at all times.

Value

Affordable and appreciated inclusion of coca tea, shampoo, Netflix and access to kitchen for food storage and heating up.

Getting around

Walkable to the centre, close to convenience stores, markets & restaurants. Tour operators are able to pick up.

Cleanliness

Clean and organized private space with a fresh, soft blanket for spending time on the couch when it gets cold overnight.

where I stayed

Accommodation review: Nature

Complete 1 bedroom unit with open-concept kitchen, dining and work space facing nature

Bed

Comfortable closed-door bedroom with plug-in radiator heating, layers of blankets, TV and natural view of large boulder.

Space

Spacious unit with separate areas for working, eating and relaxing on the couch complete with kitchen and two TVs.

Views

Partial far city view but mostly there are large rocks people can climb outside a park near ruins and green trees.

Neighbourhood

Almost at the very top of a steep incline, the neighbourhood is small and beside many natural trails and ruins to explore.

Noise

Definitely barking dogs and roosters making noise in the area but not a lot of traffic or pedestrian activity.

Host-pitality

The host met me upon arrival and helped me get into the unit. He was friendly and suggested I explore the nearby trails.

Privacy

Easy to see into unit from top of boulder outside apartment but with curtains closed, space felt private enough.

Value

Felt a bit expensive for the location being “too far” to easily order a car but unit was complete with shampoo and streaming.

Getting around

Not walkable from the centre unless you love urban hiking up lots of stairs and a very steep incline but close to one store.

Cleanliness

All spaces were spotless and the couch blanket was appreciated for the colder evenings and mornings.

Balanced reflections

Joy?
  • Ordering affordable food delivery for breakfast and dinner
  • Finding more than a handful of vegan restaurants near the centre
  • Being able to walk into the main plaza and along the old, narrow cobblestone streets
  • Seeing the rainbow flags and charming buildings flying them
  • When my first hosts checked in on my health every day and shared tips on where to eat or where to go
  • Getting to walk along a trail through Temple of the Moon ruins for free with not a lot of people around
Pain?
  • Experiencing for myself what visiting a high altitude city feels like
  • Not enjoying the taste of pepper roasted chicken and fries
  • Feeling oddly ill and having to skip the rainbow mountain tour without getting a refund or having a day to reschedule
  • The cold floors in the morning
  • Hot water in the shower being inconsistent and requiring shutting off and turning on at least once
  • Being asked for more money from the Uber driver on my way to the airport

title: Hiking at midnight
subtitle: Volcano Misti
location: Salinas y Aguada Blanca National Reserve, Peru
content:
Overnight Halloween hike to 5,822 metres

When planning to visit Arequipa, I wanted to spend half a day hiking around Volcano Misti. I knew at least one operator offered this kind of tour but didn’t realize the more common option included an overnight.

Unfortunately you need 3 other people to make the half-day option affordable so that was unlikely to happen for me.

I had completed an overnight volcanic hike 10 years earlier in Guatemala and remember it being really challenging to carry the water and really cold when starting the summit in the middle of the night. Despite the beauty of seeing sunrise above the clouds, it’s not an experience I wanted to have again. In fact I specifically avoided such a trek during my last 4-month trip away when the opportunity presented itself for Kota Kinabalu in Malaysia.

But there I was signing up to carry a backpack full of gear and water, agreeing to wake up at base camp by midnight to start the 6-hour summit the day after Halloween.

I couldn’t have come all this way to Arequipa and not gotten up close to one of the three volcanoes surrounding the beautiful city. Plus it was cheaper than a private half-day tour so felt like the only option.

I’ll have to share a tent with someone I don’t know and I considered hiring someone to carry my bag but that wasn’t affordable. The only time I’d have to carry my pack was for three hours on the first day. Summiting didn’t require carrying anything so I could look forward to that, despite how cold I know I’d be.

There would be 6 to 9 of us hiking together and in the briefing it was recommended to have 3 pairs of socks, warm gloves and hiking boots. I would bring 2 pairs of socks, regular gloves and apparently the only shoes I’d packed, the Hoka Hoparas, would not suffice. Thankfully boots were available to rent.

I’ve already considered hanging back on summit day to sleep alone in the tent but we’ll have to see how I feel and if that is an option.

The hike

After dosing myself to sleep for 9 PM and vividly dreaming for what felt like the entire time, I woke up around 6 AM to the sound of the local dog barking.

I made a smoothie and had my last poop for the next two days before energetically walking 15 minutes to the tour office. I arrived 10 minutes early, before the office was even open, eager to pack my rental bag with gear.

The only other woman who signed up didn’t show up originally, so I had to reconcile with carrying my own tent. Overall, the packed bag wasn’t as heavy as the one I took to Santa Cruz so I was confident this would be possible for me to complete.

I switched into my rented hiking boots and packed the following items into the brand new bag I was loaned:

  • sleeping bag
  • sleeping mat
  • tent
  • two pairs of gloves
  • ski pants
  • walking poles
  • a bowl, cup and fork
  • 5 litres of water
  • light snacks like trail mix, Ritz crackers, cereal bars, tortillas wrapped with peanut butter and strawberry vanilla Oreos
  • first aid kit with a variety of medication and extremity warmers
  • headlamp
  • socks
  • second layer of clothing
  • down jacket for warmth
  • rain jacket for wind
  • toque
  • buff
  • sunscreen and glasses
  • toilet paper
  • sleeping mask and ear plugs

I wore the only hiking outfit I brought on this trip, which consists entirely of merino wool: socks, underwear, a bra, a long-sleeved white top and grey joggers.

It was a little bit chaotic to organize my pack in the small office while the organizer checked off everything I was bringing on her list at the same time as attending to the other hikers but I was grateful for someone approving the gear to make sure nothing was missed.

We left later than planned so while standing around trying to avoid sitting in the middle seat, I made friends with a married German man named Florian attempting the hike for the second time. Florian was rained out when he attempted the summit three years prior and I took it as a positive sign that he was willing to go again.

Once the two 4x4 vehicles departed, we stopped in town at a mini mart for extra food, water and to use the washroom before continuing on further. I went pee twice and bought a blue Powerade for extra fuel. We stayed longer than the 5 minutes promised to wait for the women who had been late to the office earlier so I was going to be sharing the tent after all.

On the road again, we drove along the long, winding highway that cuts across the base of Chachani and passed a lot of undeveloped roads under construction. It was bumpy but manageable with my natural anti-nausea medication.

Our convoy stopped to report a dead vicuña on the road so its fur didn’t go to waste. They look like really thin llamas or alpacas and we saw a handful more on the way to volcano Misti.

The vehicles stopped once the sandy road ended and we all got out to sunscreen up and prepare to start the hike to base camp.

The two guides introduced themselves and gave us some general instructions about what to expect for the day ahead.

Despite the other woman only speaking Spanish, I made sure it was understood that we would switch carrying the tent half way through the day despite her extremely small and jam-packed bag.

I popped in my AirPods so Taylor could help me through and we started the traverse across black sandy hills, switchbacking to make the ascent more manageable. I couldn’t tell that there was an actual trail to follow so having the guide was obviously essential.

I was surprised and delighted that the 45-minute breaks came quickly. Aside from the strong wind when we started blowing sand at our faces, everything went smoothly. After the second break when I gave the tent to the other woman, I was pretty much in heaven. My bag was becoming lighter with each chug of water consumed.

At base camp, we had a couple hours to explore, set up camp and eat dinner before getting an early night’s sleep for the midnight wake up time. We enjoyed views of Pichu Pichu as the sun set and waited impatiently for the hot food to be ready to warm us up as the temperature dropped.

Short walls built from rocks divided up different areas of camp and there were large boulders further away where we could go for bathroom privacy.

Setting up the tent with my tent mate was easy enough despite not having any pegs. When I unpacked my sleeping bag and pad immediately after, I was concerned when the person I was going to be sleeping beside waited until after dark and I had already tucked in. I guess I shouldn’t have expected to sleep in any case at such a high altitude despite being tired out from the initial hike.

I was told it was okay to leave my bag with snacks outside the tent but when it started developing frost, I was nervous to wake up to cold, wet items so I fit the pack and my boots inside the tent under the foot of my sleeping bag.

When food was just about ready, we all gathered around with our borrowed dishes. The first course was quinoa soup with vegetables. I had been expecting pasta and this felt way more nutritious. I was nervous about how fast the broth cooled down and what that meant about the temperature.

I had been shivering until the next course, which for me was chicken fried rice. The guides made a large pot with fried egg, ham, chicken, rice and vegetables but I asked for a plate just with the chicken and rice. It was delicious with the added soy sauce and I started feeling warm from the protein.

Dinner was capped with a piping hot peppermint tea and I ate my Oreos alone in the tent for dessert before going to bed.

I took allergy, sleep and pain medication before putting on my sleep mask and ear plugs. For extra comfort, I made a pillow by stuffing my sleeping bag compression sack with the ski pants and my rain coat but I stayed bundled up in my down jacket, hat, buff, gloves, second pair of socks and clothing. Despite my best efforts, I don’t think I slept at all.

My tent mate wasn’t too disturbing when she came in and I was very conscious of the noise I was making by breathing. I think the altitude made it harder for me than usual to breathe silently. I tried to stay in one position but I kept rotating when my hips started to hurt or when my hands started to lose feeling. At one point I heard snoring so I left the tent to pee and was surprised it wasn’t as cold as I thought it would be. And the stars were incredible!

Around 12:30 AM we were woken up by the guides asking if we were okay outside the tent. I felt fine, even energized to start preparing for the hike. I was shocked I wasn’t feeling tired or sick. I guess some of the hikers didn’t have a great night and elected to not summit because of altitude sickness. You just never know who it’s going to hit!

I put on my windbreaker, ski pants and headlamp before leaving the tent to brush my teeth and tried to poop unsuccessfully twice before drinking two cups of coca tea. My bag was repacked with just snacks and water. I took the bread with butter, jam and queso fresco for breakfast to go.

We started the 6-hour summit hike around 1 AM and were told every hour there would be a short rest. If after two hours anyone was feeling ill, they could return to base camp.

The first hour was a gradual incline perfect for breaking everyone into the day. I felt confident I could do this but after that, it got harder. We walked across loose sand and gravel in darkness during the first three hours. Every break was a great relief but the cold set in after a few seconds so they didn’t last long. The half moon was bright and all the hikers kept pace with one another until the last two hours.

Unlike the first day, when the breaks seemed to come quickly, the second day’s breaks didn’t come frequently enough for me. Not even Taylor, the sunrise or beauty of snow-capped volcanoes was helping.

As we ascended, I started to notice it became harder to breathe deeply and began coughing. I would be lying if I said I didn’t contemplate going back down.

At the fourth break, I hyperventilated into tears and was overwhelmed with the physical feat I had committed to. I had a couple pieces of bread but wasn’t able to stomach much else so my energy was low and the tiredness was setting in. I asked one of our guides if we were close but he said no! I was distraught.

Vowing to continue from then on at my own slower pace, there was only one more hour until we could see the cross on the summit. I remembered reading a blog post from someone who did the same hike who said that once they saw the cross, they knew they’d summit. I guess I had the same feeling but the top still felt incredibly far for the pace I was going.

I crossed one half of a switchback and stopped for a brief rest over and over until the final ascent next to a thin line of snow. I was the last one to make it but I felt relief that all the hardest parts of the adventure were over.

The crater was vast and had a little bit of smoke activity coming from one side. The views of Arequipa, Chachani and other volcanoes in the distance were epic but the effort endured didn’t quite feel worth it to me.

When there are active volcanic parks you can walk around in places like Japan and Hawaii, summiting doesn’t really feel necessary.

So I won’t be pushing my body like this again.

After everyone was done taking their pictures and videos, we started the descent a different, more direct way down. It took about 2 hours to slide through the steep sandy edges of volcano Misti and despite the incredibly helpful hiking poles, my knees were shaking by the time we got back to base camp.

The amount of sand that found its way into my boots, socks and pant legs was hilarious. We took a few breaks to take off the layers that kept us warm on the way up but it was hard to find a place for rest along the slippery slopes.

Once back at base camp, I retired immediately to my tent to rest my legs and organize my pack for the hike back down to the vehicles. We had 30 minutes before having to leave so I tried my best to move slowly while packing up all the gear.

I had some crackers, went pee and worked with the person I shared the tent with to fold it back into its bag. She ended up carrying it the entire way down because there were no breaks. It took less than an hour to descend directly down the soft slopes and it was fun taking the huge deep steps. I enjoyed passing by the colourful lava rocks and was relieved to see the vehicles waiting for us at the bottom with fresh fruit for the ride home.

I think everyone was pretty eager to get out of there. Thirteen hours of hiking in 24 hours was a lot.

I took anti-nausea medication as a precaution for the bumpy, windy ride home and dozed off for a portion of it with everyone else. When we arrived back in the city, I returned all the rented gear, switched back into my Hoka Hoparas and packed my smaller bag for the quick walk home.

It was Sunday, November 1st and not much was open due to the holiday. The first thing I did after arriving back at the Airbnb was shower to get all the sand off of me. I will hand wash my clothing tomorrow. Then I got into bed and tried to order pizza from Rappi but nothing was available for delivery because all the drivers were with their families remembering loved ones who had passed.

I ate the rest of my crackers and trail mix while rechecking the app every hour for my delivery options. Once I got through to place an order, I unpacked and cleaned my space while waiting for the margarita pizza to arrive. I ate the entire thing and it was delicious. After brushing my teeth and catching up on floss, I fell asleep by 6:30 PM and slept for 12 whole hours until awoken like every morning by the barking dog living on the first floor.

Feelings check

After learning the half-day hike on Volcano Misti wouldn’t be possible without three other people signing up or paying $200 USD, I felt pressure to pivot so my trip to Arequipa wouldn’t be wasted.

I knew that no matter what, I would have a great time exploring the city without any grand volcanic excursion but there were so many tour operators, I still felt like I had to secure something.

I was concerned when every overnight tour involved carrying your own gear but felt it would be manageable when I found one option that would only require 3 hours of hiking for the first day. I was in disbelief when I agreed to wake up at midnight for the second 6-hour day of hiking but trusted that because the tour was being offered, it would be possible.

I felt much better and less emotional than when starting the Santa Cruz trek likely because it was only going to be one night so that was a good sign.

I was relieved when the gear I rented was great quality and the overall weight of my bag wasn’t unmanageable even with the 5 litres of water and tent. I now know not to pack heavy snacks like apples and carrots.

My plan was to take medication to get a full 8 hours of sleep before the second day of hiking so I was a little annoyed when we left later than usual and waited for the woman who had been late.

After the first hour and a half of hiking, I was elated when giving my tent mate the tent to carry. It felt like heaven.

I also really appreciated connecting with the married German man, Florian, because it felt like we were looking out for each other’s health and wellness during that day and a half together.

The food provided for dinner at base camp was very satisfying and it felt good to not have to worry about a lack of energy for the next day of hiking. Being hungry on that first day felt like a good sign.

I was surprised that I wasn’t grumpy when waking up in the dark on that second day and was relieved to feel energized to continue the ascent. Panic only started to set in when I started coughing, feeling tired, hungry and very aware of how steep the trail we were walking was right before the sun started to rise.

The views were cool but not nearly the best I’d ever seen, so I feel ungrateful saying they weren’t really good enough to keep me motivated but it’s the truth. I love volcanic landscapes but hiking up to 5,800 metres pushed my body past its limits and doesn’t feel necessary when getting up close without summiting would have been sufficient.

I think it’s okay to be done with camping, sleeping in my outdoor gear and waking up in the dark to climb when I know it’s not enjoyable. I don’t want to suffer or put myself at risk of injury or sickness.

I love long walks along flat ground while looking at nature and not carrying anything so hopefully I can remember not to deviate from that too much in the future.

I know high altitude activities feel natural to a lot of people but I can’t understand why humans go places that make them feel sick or in pain from lack of oxygen. I don’t need to prove anything to myself or anyone else. I just want to enjoy the ease life can offer.

Summiting volcano Misti was the hardest thing I’ve ever experienced and I know I wasn’t the only hiker who felt that way. I can’t even say the hike was rewarding. It was just hard. I appreciated the leg workout but soon after day two started, I knew this wasn’t something I wanted to do again.

on the trail

Trail review

A sandy climb higher than Everest Base Camp surrounded by 3 different Arequipa volcanoes

Cost

500 soles (~$206 CAD) for 4x4 transportation, appropriate gear, two tour guides, dinner, breakfast and snacks.

Length

Goes from 4,100 m to base camp at 4,750 m over 3 hours (~7 km), then up to 5,800 m in 6 hours and back down in 3 hours (~11 km).

Difficulty

The second day was extremely strenuous because of the high altitude, lack of sleep and little food. The first day was okay.

Views

Sandy volcanic slopes dotted with spiky yellow bushes, tiny green succulents and volcanoes Pichu Pichu and Chachani.

People

Only our small group was on the side of the volcano we were climbing and staying on. Everyone was friendly and respectful.

Transportation

4x4 vehicles are required to traverse across the sandy, bumpy desert road and it feels necessary to hire someone to find the way.

Weather

Moderate temperature in the day with full clothing coverage needed to protect against sun and wind but below freezing overnight and frigid before sunrise. No rain!

Terrain

Soft, black volcanic sand and loose gravel switchbacks on the way up. Solid ground was rare. Deep sand steps coming down.

Requirements

Warm outdoor layers, mental perseverance, high altitude tolerance and willingness to push your body to the limit.

Amenities

No food source, water, established bathroom or shelter but lots of large bushes and boulders creating privacy.

Balanced reflections

Joy?
  • Spending a lot of time outside and up close in volcanic landscapes
  • Learning I’d only have to carry my full pack for 3 hours on the first day
  • When breaks on the first day seemed to come quickly
  • Coming home after the hardest adventure I’ve ever experienced
  • Any time the trail had a flat break and it felt easy to be where I was
  • Seeing the pink sunset light up the surrounding volcanoes, the bright half moon while summiting after midnight and endless stars after sunset
  • The delicious base camp arroz chaufa cooked for me that I didn’t have to pick egg out from
  • Feeling warm and protected from the elements in the ski pants, boots and gloves provided
  • Having a memorable Halloween on the side of a volcano
  • Receiving fresh fruit at the end of the hike before riding home
Pain?
  • Having to accept I needed to do a 2D/1N hike in order to see Misti and realizing the half-day experience was not popular or offered by more than one operator
  • Realizing I would need to carry all my own gear and 5 litres of water
  • Not finding one comfortable position to sleep in the tent
  • Dying for a hike break during summit day but freezing 30 seconds after we’d stop
  • Not being able to take deep breaths while resting at base camp
  • Developing a cough while ascending after sunrise on day two
  • Feeling like I wanted to turn around and that I wouldn’t finish the hike because of the altitude
  • Learning we weren’t watching the sunrise from the summit
  • When my knees were becoming jelly on the way down from the summit and being too exhausted to hold myself up

title: “Yes, stay”
subtitle: in the city made from volcanic stone
content:
Volcanic cities are the coolest

When I first arrived in Arequipa, I felt different being here compared to Huaraz, Lima and Mexico City.

Maybe it was due to the fact that I’d been away from home for over a month now and the transition period was finally over. But I think it’s because I was staying in a student area near one of the universities and didn’t feel like I was standing out to locals so no one was paying me much attention when I walked to and from the closest grocery store on my first night here.

After sunset in the middle of the week, the streets were busy with young people trying to catch buses or colectivos and there were outdoor markets selling prepared food, specialty items, clothing, trinkets and plants.

My end-of-the-street accommodation was really comfortable and aside from the small dog living on the first floor alerting everyone living in the complex when people were coming and going, it seemed quiet.

The buildings were all charming, made of white, pink and black volcanic stone, complete with significant carvings and old gates. There were little manicured parkettes and cobblestone roads blocked off from cars the way into the main square, Plaza de Armas.

The old streets were lined with hidden squares and rooftop patios with food appealing to tourists and endless companies ready to help you plan an adventure in nature.

I would be here for more than a week so I decided to order grocery delivery with Rappi on my first full day from a few different places to get everything I needed. With the help of AI, I wanted to make a hearty, vegetable-packed spicy peanut stew so picked out local spices I hadn’t heard of before and the rocoto pepper for added heat.

My spicy, garlic, potato, chickpea, bell pepper, frozen pea and fresh carrot dish finished with cilantro and lime was so satisfying, I ate it for four days in a row before starting the Halloween Misti Volcano overnight hike.

The main reason I had chosen to visit Arequipa was to get up close to Volcano Misti.

From my research, I knew there was a half-day tour available but when I talked to a handful of the tour operators, no one seemed to offer such a short length on Misti. The company I did visit who offered the half-day tour would only be able to do so affordably with a total of four people and it was unlikely three others would sign up in the next week.

So I decided on a 2-day, 1-night summit hike and you can read about how that went in the next post!

To prepare for the hike, I browsed AllTrails to see what kind of walks were around me. I found a moderately rated 10 km trail starting at the main Plaza de Armas that follows the Chili River with views of all three volcanoes surrounding Arequipa. I walked outside of the city through rural farm areas and then up to a lookout that cost 5 soles where I had some sparkling water and a pisco sour. There was also a washroom to use and stores to browse with trinkets and wool.

I walked during the day in the middle of the week so no one was really on the trail. I saw a few families near one part of the river where kids were playing in the water while their parents did laundry. One couple was in front of me for a short period of time looking for a nice place to have lunch.

I marvelled at the snow-covered Misti volcano and loved seeing it tower over the many different foregrounds I walked past.

On my way back down the trail, I passed a few solo walkers and some couples on motorcycles. Overall, the trail was enjoyable despite the few mosquito bites on my uncovered legs.

I spent a lot of time in my Airbnb before the Halloween Misti Volcano hike resting, watching Netflix and consuming all my groceries. I tried a passion fruit cheesecake cinnamon bun and was really into spicy Takis, microwaved popcorn and strawberry filled cookies.

Every day there was a bit of construction noise coming from neighbours in the building and during the loudest time I went out to speak to a man to ask when the noise would end. How was I in another Airbnb with people living beside me doing construction? I noticed music being played out loud during the day so that was also really distracting. The reversing noise of vehicles or acceleration of trucks squeezing into the small alleyway to drop off construction materials was frustrating. Of course the glass windows and wooden door are not soundproof.

After the hike, I kind of did the same thing except I relied more on meal delivery during my recovery.

I really enjoyed snuggling up in the soft blankets on the couch writing and relaxing while waiting to try different foods. The first day back I ordered and ate an entire margarita pizza. The day after that I tried a pizza with tomato, cheese, gooseberries, pecans, sesame seeds and two spicy salsas!

I booked a free walking tour for my last full day during sunset and learned a ton about the city I had been staying in.

There were a few other people waiting for the same tour but they left because the guide was pretty late. I had taken a bit of an edible and was flying to Cusco the next day so was pretty keen to complete the tour that evening.

So the guide and I walked together around town. He explained the architecture influences of the beautiful buildings, squares and alleyways. I learned how 4th- or 5th-generation Arequipeños don’t consider themselves Peruvian and there is some separatist history in the country. I was grateful to hear about how to spot a real picantería and even went back to one after the tour to try authentic, spicy Arequipeño food and drink.

I wish I took the tour at the start of my visit so I would have had more time to go back exploring all the areas I was shown. I saw photos of the classic local foods and I really wanted to try all the vegetarian ones.

I commemorated my final evening with a plate of cauche de queso, a pisco sour and queso helado! Every bite was spectacular. The spicy, cheesy, potato dish was so comforting and I took half home for breakfast the next day. I was so happy they served the ice cream I was told about on my walking tour. The milky, cinnamon spiced treat was a perfect end to a great meal.

I loved that there were only a few other people in the restaurant and that it was inside an old gated square, so it felt quite hidden.

After dropping my leftovers at home, I went back out to find water because the water where I was staying and in other areas of the city had been out since 6 AM and wouldn’t be back until 11 PM. I appreciated being able to wash my hands a few times at the picantería.

I really loved how lively the areas I walked through were and again left feeling very comfortable amongst the younger population of students.

I walked home with my final small bag of Fuego Takis and planned to pack, wash and prepare to leave the next day. My host was gracious enough to let me stay until 4 PM without booking another full day so I’d have lots of time to take the garbage out and do the dishes.

I ordered one last meal from Rappi for lunch before going to the airport and enjoyed two more kinds of fantastic flambéed maki rolls.

Arequipa means “yes, stay” and I would definitely come back and stay for longer :)

Feelings check

Relief and ease washed over me the moment I left my Airbnb on the first night in Arequipa. I headed straight to the grocery store while FaceTiming with my Oma and breezed through the busy street without a shred of anxiety.

I was feeling extra connected when the younger guy I met in Lima also called me while I was browsing the grocery store and we talked about the possibility of meeting up in Cusco. After hanging up with Claudio, I also really enjoyed asking the tall, hot student in the yogurt section to help me find something lactose-free.

The relief continued when not one insect was in my living space and I could cook without urgency or worry. I loved trying the local ingredients and spices.

Going for a trail walk that felt safe and remote with endless volcanic views was therapeutic and sipping another pisco sour halfway through before the tourist group showed up was so relaxing.

I felt really uneasy about my decision to sign up for an overnight hike but panicked about not having time to find a suitable alternative option when the half-day trek wasn’t widely offered. I put pressure on myself to follow through on a version of my original plans and I need to remember it’s okay when things have to change.

It’s always a good reminder that I can do hard things but when you choose them and they require a wild amount of effort that has the potential to injure or make you sick, I don’t see the point.

At 35, I’ve lived a full, incredible life and everything during this trip is a bonus so anything easy feels like the better choice for joy.

With such a big world, there is no way I’m going to be able to walk along every trail so I have to remember the small subset I have experienced and will be satisfied with that.

I was so happy to be on the way back home from the hardest thing I’ve ever experienced (the Volcano Misti overnight hike) and have never been more certain that I never want to do anything at such a high altitude again.

I find so much satisfaction in ordering food delivery with Rappi because it’s so affordable compared to Canada. I love not having to actually dress and go out for food because it keeps the experience low sensory for me.

The noise of construction, music out loud, people and barking dogs still drives me into a silent rage but I think with time I am managing better. I felt a little awkward expressing my dissatisfaction to the neighbour when the sound of him moving aluminum-type siding became too much but better when I asked him about the name of the dog and gave him my leftover groceries before checking out.

I really appreciate when soft blankets to curl up outside the bed are provided and this apartment had three! I feel at home when I can watch Netflix or my shows on a comfortable couch so it was bittersweet to leave because of that.

At least one meal in public feels like a great way to commemorate visiting a new city and I was grateful the walking tour guide recommended a charming picantería where I could try and enjoy new foods.

Arequipa left a great taste in my mouth and it’s definitely somewhere I would return for longer. Everyone was friendly, there are still more local dishes I need to try and nothing is better than a city surrounded by volcanoes!

where I stayed

Accommodation review

Comfortable studio apartment with soft blankets and a small washroom in a quiet area

Bed

Easy to fall asleep in with two pillows, classic sheets, a nice duvet, accent pillow and two side lamps for mood lighting.

Space

Studio apartment with spacious sleeping area, lots of storage, dining room table, functional kitchen and hot water shower.

Views

Views of neighbouring building and dead-end street below which provides some natural light and quiet.

Neighbourhood

Safe area at the end of street near charming buildings, parkettes and only a 13-minute walk to the main square.

Noise

Cara the small dog living in the complex barks anytime someone enters or leaves and the neighbour was doing construction.

Host-pitality

Very friendly and proactive with checking in to ask if I needed anything and provided clear instructions for entry.

Privacy

Can see some windows across the way when bedroom area curtains are open but the higher floor feels somewhat private.

Value

Very affordable for somewhere so close to the centre and in a relatively quiet area and I appreciated the water and chocolates.

Getting around

Affordable Didis to and from airport available but main plaza, restaurants, markets and grocery stores all close by.

Cleanliness

Clean but needed mopping and gathered lint from the bath towels after use that required consistent sweeping.

Balanced reflections

Joy?
  • Finally feeling comfortable out in public for the first time since leaving home
  • Being wrapped in soft blankets like I would be at home while watching Netflix and ordering or eating delicious food
  • Walking through Arequipa and marvelling at the volcanic stone buildings
  • Exploring trails on my own with not many other people around and feeling safe doing so
  • Cooking with new spicy ingredients and trying delicious local foods
  • Seeing massive volcanoes from every direction while being anywhere outside
Pain?
  • Walking into the complex to a local dog barking and hearing it every morning before 6 AM
  • Learning I’d have to carry my own camping gear and water to Volcano Misti
  • Hiking hungry in the cold and dark before dawn at altitudes higher than Everest Base Camp
  • Hearing loud construction noise on multiple occasions from the neighbour in the building
  • When the water was off in many parts of the city, including where I was staying, from 6 AM to 11 PM
  • When I couldn’t easily handwash the volcanic sand out of my hiking socks and I had to sweep multiple times

title: Warding off romantic advances
subtitle: from someone younger and someone older
content:
It’s too early to be connecting with people

After the horrific night bus experience from Huaraz filled with vomit and poop, I was excited to be back in Lima at my last-minute accommodation which claimed to be in a quiet, gated park. The two-bedroom apartment was on the top of a 3-storey building and had floor-to-ceiling glass doors that opened onto a terrace overlooking the manicured park. The king bed, natural light and subscription TV in both rooms were the perfect place to recover, order food and to cook.

Before I even crossed through the gates, I noticed the amount of tiny ants outside crawling on the ground and on top of ledges bordering the gardens. I was concerned because I had to put my bag down while waiting for the Didi driver to come back and accept the change I had finally procured to pay for my ride from the bus station.

Unfortunately the ants were present in the beautiful Airbnb and seemed to be adamant about burrowing inside my things, no matter where I stored them. They were on the kitchen counter, dining room table, desk areas, the floor around the door, in the bathroom and even in the wardrobes once I put my bag in them. Only the beds seemed like safe spaces so I spent the first 2 days in them watching Netflix and Prime.

I reached out to the host immediately to ask for solutions given I planned to be there for 10 days and wanted to order food for cooking. The host arranged for someone to come with poison powder the next day and that seemed to be effective. When dead ants lined the floor the following day, someone came to mop. I only saw a few ants every day after that so the problem became manageable and they were contained to the kitchen counter, not roaming around my keyboard or clothing.

I considered finding another place to stay and that would have been a cheaper option but I ultimately stuck it out because I really liked the apartment and didn’t want to pack up again to move.

I was a little disappointed that you do hear quite a bit of noise every day and night from barking dogs and maintenance workers but I figured anywhere else I found would be worse because of traffic and honking. Nights were peaceful with the white noise of the fan, my earplugs and the extra background noise from the phone to drown out the early morning dog walkers and chirping birds.

When I felt strong enough after filling up on Indian food for the first two days, I was ready to go outside for a walk.

I walked to Kennedy Park and followed a trail from AllTrails that connected to the water and back. I stopped for a moment to peek over the cliffside down at the ocean below and a man with a bike approached me. I think he was asking about Italian food restaurants nearby but maybe I misheard. He was a local and continued to engage me in conversation, asking where I was from, if I had siblings and how long I’d be visiting.

His name was Hans, he was older than me and every inch of his skin was protected from the sun. I charmingly couldn’t help but complain immediately about the noise and how I’d become sick from drinking the water so wasn’t ready to join him for a pisco sour or any kind of food that night when he asked.

I reluctantly gave him my number and continued on with my walk, agreeing to make plans with him later in the week.

At the same time, Claudio, the younger person I met a few weeks ago when walking in Barranco, was asking to make plans now that I was back in Lima unexpectedly for the next week.

I thought he was sweet to be checking in with me while I had been hiking in Huaraz so I looked forward to seeing him again despite how hands-on with me he had been during our first meeting.

I kept the work week to myself for cooking and exploring on my own. On Friday I rented a bike and explored the entirety of the 22 km oceanfront trail from past Barranco to beyond San Miguel.

I finally saw some sandy beaches like the very popular Agua Dulce but I didn’t make it up the hill towards Morro Solar where all the statues are. I liked how there were little places to get food along the sidewalk and that things were being sold on the beach.

The trail wasn’t seamlessly connected until after Miraflores and the further north you rode, the fewer people were around. Many of the beaches were closed due to construction or safety so there weren’t any opportunities to walk barefoot along the shore. A lot of them were also unfortunately filled with garbage.

It was really interesting to see the change in infrastructure and development from the south to north coast go from modern high-rises to more self-built, working-class coastal districts.

I found the bike ride towards the north very easy with the wind pushing me forward as the sun was setting over San Lorenzo Island. I wish I had more time to walk along the coast to La Punta but I was eager to turn around before it got dark.

Biking back in the wind was challenging but I loved that no one was around. It wasn’t too long before I reached San Miguel and could take my bike back up to the cliffside path without having to carry it over stairs.

I had hoped to be able to ride the Costa Verde path all the way back to Miraflores but I ended up riding along the street. Google Maps wasn’t providing bike directions and I didn’t think to consult the AllTrails maps which have bike markings so I alternated between following the driving and walking directions.

It was chaotic because in some walking areas like parks, you aren’t allowed to ride or the adjacent roads are one-way only. At one point when weaving through traffic, I hit a driver’s side mirror but thankfully it was a parked car so no one yelled at me. Other than that, I made it home unscathed.

The next day I had made plans with both Hans and Claudio. I told Hans that I wasn’t looking to hook up and if he was expecting that, to stay home. I told Claudio that I was wary of hanging out with him in my Airbnb when he suggested bringing over dinner the night before because of his persistence in trying to touch me when we first met.

In any case, the men agreed to move forward with plans to meet.

I wanted to try ceviche and my first ever pisco sour so found a recommendation in Miraflores from my favourite AI, Claude. I invited Hans to join me for the occasion.

First of all, the ceviche was AMAZING. Everything I ate in Peru was truly outstanding as expected. I ate at Barra Maretazo because of their ceviche, chicharrón and pisco sour combo. I read that they also offered free appetizers. I was excited to get a little taste of everything!

So I made a reservation for 2 PM and met Hans out front. There wasn’t a lot of airflow inside the restaurant and Hans was covered up for sun protection so seemed uncomfortable the entire time with his layers. He mentioned how expensive the place I picked was and how he usually makes everything at home, even ceviche. I said we could share my order and decided I’d pay for the one drink he had while I ate most of the meal.

When we sat down the waiter brought us roasted Andean corn to start. Then they prepared two single bites of white fish ceviche and a Peruvian roasted potato with sauce for each of us. Both were delicious. I ordered the combo of ceviche and calamari with a passion fruit pisco sour. The dish came with sweet potato, fresh Andean corn and some yucca fries. I really enjoyed the spicy red sauce that was provided and ate it with everything. I think the other white sauce was mayo-based.

I likely would have had a better time eating by myself given Hans’ attitude and personality but I persevered in getting to know him. He showed me photos of his art and some of the clay pipes he had made, which opened the conversation up to marijuana. I told him I did smoke weed and he said he did have some so at least I would get some tokes out of this interaction.

I didn’t love learning that he was anti-vax and there were many lulls in our conversation where he asked me the same questions from when we first interacted.

When lunch was over and we both used the washroom, it was time for a little walk to find a nice place to smoke. Oddly, he didn’t have a lighter and I was surprised when he made me purchase one.

We found a place inside a manicured park along the cliffside path to sit under a tree and he packed the pipe with weed for us. I probably had 5 tokes before wanting to move on to my plans with Claudio. I can’t say I really got high but it felt good to smoke again after an entire month.

Apparently Hans also provides massages and he really liked my red socks so gave me a brief foot rub. I told him I was meeting another friend and he didn’t seem too happy about that. I guess he planned to spend the entire day and night with me despite never communicating those intentions. I told him we could bike together the following day to appease him.

We walked together for a bit longer and he asked if we could take a photo together. I said okay and then he gave someone his phone to capture us. I don’t know who he is going to brag to about our time together but I looked terrible in every photo and didn’t ask him to send them to me. Of course by the end of our hangout, he snuck a kiss on my lips without my enthusiastic consent so that was unfortunate.

I was happy to end our interaction and headed to the main square in Barranco to meet Claudio. I stopped for my first pumpkin-spice-themed drink of the season from Starbucks and found a place to sit, waiting for Claudio.

He approached me from behind and looked extremely suave if I’m being honest. I was dressed in a somewhat ridiculous red crop tank and shorts outfit that drew constant attention and was the subject of much banter between us. He was wearing light-coloured khaki pants and a button-down shirt with comfy slide-like shoes and socks.

I know that locals are more covered up than tourists but the temperature was so warm that I was never cold. I was grateful to be walking with a local for the protection against the looks I was receiving.

I still didn’t know how old Claudio was and he continued to lie to me about his age. At one point he told me 35 and I asked him what year he was born but he evaded the question. I know he’s in his 20s and it doesn’t really matter but it’s weird he won’t tell me. Despite him correcting my posture at one point, we were getting along well and having a good time together.

I told Claudio about my autism and how I really enjoyed exploring a water’s edge so we walked further south along the coast than I had made it the day before on my bike to the base of Morro Solar after dark. During many points he had held my hand, put his arms around me during seated breaks and tried to kiss my lips. I didn’t mind our bodies touching but I wasn’t ready to let it go further despite his advances to have sex on the beach.

At the end of our trail, we discussed taking a car back into town to make our way to Lima central for pisco sours. A few days earlier Claudio had sent me an Instagram reel of massive drinks at a hotel bar that we could go to. He suggested I go back to my place to shower and change, then he would meet me there so we could take transit to the bar. There was no chance I had the energy to go home, shower and go out again so we enjoyed listening to the waves in each other’s arms and slowly made our way back to Barranco.

We walked past a lot of cockroaches hanging out on the ledge of the cliffside trail onto the sandy beach shore of Agua Dulce and I couldn’t believe how lively it was even after 10 PM. There was an outdoor movie area set up selling popcorn and vendors offering other food and drink. Families were running around and couples were cuddled up. I would not have been able to see this without my local escort.

I bought a bag of popcorn for our walk back because I hadn’t eaten or had water since my 2 PM lunch and learned Claudio doesn’t like popcorn. It started to rain but I still wasn’t cold.

After making it back to Barranco, we went to a convenience store for Gatorade before I called a car to bring me back to San Isidro.

I wouldn’t be seeing Claudio again because he had plans the following day and I was leaving the day after that. If we did have more time, I would have enjoyed being naked together but it doesn’t seem like that will be happening.

When I arrived home, I ordered cheesy bread delivery from Little Caesars and prepared for the bike ride I wanted to take on Sunday.

I didn’t realize this but on Sundays, some of the streets are closed to cars in the morning for bikers so on Arequipa Avenue I rode as far as the bike trail led into Lima central. I thought about parking to grab another pisco sour at the hotel bar I missed out on the previous night but ultimately decided to ride back past the outdoor markets, return my bike and find sushi.

Lima has a network of city bikes I considered renting and I kept trying to pass someone riding one on my way back. For a few blocks, the man on the city bike and I rode beside each other and chatted in English about how my bike was clearly faster. He was from Brazil and I considered continuing to ride onwards to the ocean with him because he was cute but I returned my bike instead.

I messaged Hans and told him where I’d be eating lunch in case he wanted to join me after for a walk and I apologized for biking without him. I walked 30 minutes to Maketto Lima and ordered spicy edamame, a torched maki roll and flambéed salmon belly nigiri. I was feeling brave about raw fish after the ceviche and really enjoyed the light cook of flambéed sushi. The meal was expensive and I wanted so much more than what I ordered after loving it so much.

Right as I finished up, Hans arrived and we walked back towards Miraflores together. I didn’t bring the lighter he made me buy and of course he still didn’t have one on him so we couldn’t smoke together. I kept the interaction short after he found us a spot to sit under a tree because it genuinely felt like a waste of time to be with him.

I wanted to get home to pack and enjoy my last hours in the Airbnb so I said goodbye and under my breath, good riddance.

Back in San Isidro, I ordered another maki roll for dinner. It was delicious. The inside of most rolls seems to be shrimp tempura and avocado or cream cheese with different sauces and fish toppings. I want to try them all.

At this point I had run out of toilet paper despite receiving an extra roll days earlier. I saved a few squares for my final poop but for the last 12 hours before I departed, I had to use a white hand towel for my pee and my own hands to blow my nose. I’ve run into this issue with needing more toilet paper 3 times now so maybe it’s time to consciously cut back on my usage going forward.

Feelings check

I was relieved to have such a beautiful Airbnb to recover in with the table space and natural light needed for productive work. The ants were an uncomfortable setback but the high quality linens and Amazon Prime access for nonstop SVU watching were delightful. I wished the apartment had more floors because when the shades were open, it was a bit awkward to see people looking up when they were running and walking by. The kitchen stove top was extremely efficient and cooking food after getting grocery delivery was a joy.

I loved how affordable delivery with Rappi and Didi was, despite no delivery person being able to bring anything directly to my door given the park gates and unusual place for housing.

It felt good to reconnect live with my best friend and to put a plan in place for more open communication moving forward. I need to try and release my reliance on my neighbour’s and other people’s attention for feeling at ease travelling on my own.

I still don’t have the energy levels to leave the house every day but I am finally in a comfortable enough place to take a bit of the weed edibles I smuggled with me. It’s the medicine I need to help me stay outside longer without the exhaustion of social anxiety.

When I notice people trying to get my attention while walking despite having my AirPods, hat and sunglasses on, the masking it takes for me to politely smile or speak back to them is draining. I think that’s why I can only handle a few days outside per week.

It was very satisfying to explore tens of kilometres of oceanfront trail on the bike I rented and on foot. There is so much to explore in Lima but I found myself returning to streets or places I had already been for comfort and confidence navigating. I think that’s also an autism thing.

I want to work on not fostering connection with people just because they approach me and for it to be easier to say no when people ask for my number.

I know it’s important and enriching to meet people when travelling and to have shared experiences but when it feels like I’m only approached for my appearance, I don’t like it. I prefer to be the one initiating relationships based on shared interests and not attractiveness.

After casually texting with Claudio over 3 weeks and spending 7 hours together walking, I grew fond of his company. I even invited him to meet me in Cusco in a couple of weeks. I felt comfortable spending time with him because it distracted me from everyone we passed by that paid me any kind of attention.

The barking dogs were inescapable but Lima as a city grew on me the more time I spent there.

where I stayed

Accommodation review

Naturally lit 2-bedroom apartment in gated park community with king bed, terrace & ants

Bed

Both the king and queen beds were very comfortable with warm duvets and several pillows with cases that didn’t quite fit.

Space

Open studio with the king bed, terrace, work stations, wardrobe and bathroom storage with a full second bedroom.

Views

Floor-to-ceiling green manicured park views from the main area with tweeting colourful birds and pedestrians enjoying the area.

Neighbourhood

Safely inside the gated Parque José Luis Bustamante y Rivero which is patrolled around the clock by security guards.

Noise

Away from traffic and honking cars but still in earshot of barking residential dogs, families and early morning bird chirps.

Host-pitality

Friendly and responsive to the issues I experienced with the ants, in needing more toilet paper and fresh washcloths.

Privacy

People can see in the apartment when the blinds are open and when on the terrace but it’s private when blinds are closed.

Value

Two bottles of water and chocolates were provided but more toilet paper was needed and it felt expensive for having ants.

Getting around

Walkable to restaurants, convenience stores and popular areas like Miraflores and Barranco in 30 minutes.

Cleanliness

Pretty clean aside from the roaming ants and could have used a good mop before I checked in.

Balanced reflections

Joy?
  • Food and grocery delivery to minimize being in public
  • Cooking ravioli with peppers, garlic bread and Caesar salad
  • Being surrounded by natural light
  • Biking along the coast and on the Arequipa Avenue centre bike lane
  • Eating Indian food, ceviche, calamari and maki rolls
  • Watching endless Law and Order: Special Victims Unit
  • Walking with edibles and getting to smoke a little bit of weed
  • Staying out late on the beach with Claudio
  • Getting a late check out to fully enjoy the space I was in before heading to the airport
Pain?
  • Remaining vigilant about the ants and having to constantly kill them
  • People able to see inside the apartment with the blinds open
  • Time with Hans talking about things that did not interest me
  • Biking along the road in the dark during traffic without bike paths
  • Feeling gross the day after eating Little Caesars cheesy bread products
  • Being asked about my weight and having my posture corrected
  • Not having enough toilet paper to blow my nose or pee
  • Feeling dependent on Daniel’s attention for my happiness
  • Unwanted touching and attention from locals

title: So much vomit, poop and crying
subtitle: Santa Cruz Trek
content:
If you start off crying, you probably shouldn’t go

When your period is coming, it’s harder to do things that are out of the ordinary. I don’t mean to blame my menstrual cycle for all of my emotions but the patterns have been clear.

When I picked up my rental gear for the first solo multi-day trek I’d ever do, I was excited. The backpack, tent, sleeping bag and kitchen gear felt light and I was sure after packing my food and clothing that Santa Cruz was something I would enjoy.

I updated my close circle of friends and family, telling them I’d be offline for the next few days and when to expect to hear from me again if all went well.

I had confirmed my pickup transportation, set an alarm and planned to be asleep by 8 PM for the 5 AM pickup.

Once my bag was packed, the panic set in. The weight was a lot on my back. I probably shouldn’t have brought apples, carrots and grapes but the fresh food felt important to have for the next 4 days.

I exploded into tears before bed, hyperventilating over the thought of being alone doing something really hard for such a long time.

I knew the trek would be beautiful and rewarding but being weighed down by my choice of carrying everything started to feel like the wrong choice. I could have elected to hike with a group where donkeys are used for carrying the heaviest of everyone’s gear but I was adamant about having my solo experience.

I slept well but was concerned when I didn’t hear from my transportation contact double confirming the pick up time and location. At 4:30 AM I started to get ready not sure anyone would actually be coming to get me and at 5 AM, hoping something got lost in translation.

But at 5:02 AM down my quiet residential street came a honking colectivo waking up more than just the dogs, I’m sure. So I went outside with my huge bag and tucked into the bench of seats behind the driver.

During the 2-hour drive to Caraz I cried silently due to overstimulation between trying to get some extra sleep while people got in and out of the van. My leg space was restricted because of the bag and I wish I’d sat in one of the single seats to avoid the feeling of people brushing up against me.

The van emptied before the final hour to the trailhead and I saw a couple dressed in hiking attire with their own large packs about to board. I cried immediately in front of them before saying anything else, trying to explain quickly that I was overwhelmed and nervous about carrying the weight of my bag on the hike we were all heading to.

I learned they were from the French part of Switzerland and were travelling together for an entire year after having given up their jobs and apartment. Watching them eat breakfast reminded me to start eating before the van continued on so after some fruit and a jam croissant, I napped to help myself calm down.

When we arrived near the trailhead, I planned to hike in with the couple but thought at some point I’d detach to let them go ahead without me, knowing I’d be extremely slow and not wanting to hold them back.

There was no one at the gate to check in with or to pay a park fee to so we started up the gentle incline together.

After what felt like a few minutes, I told them I was going to pee and that they should continue on. They mentioned waiting but I insisted they go. After packing out my toilet paper I saw them again not too far away and at that point it was settled, without a word, that we’d be hiking together.

I feel like they adopted me because of my emotional outburst.

We passed cows, men leading donkeys and cacti trees while following the Santa Cruz river.

It was Canadian Thanksgiving so during one of our breaks to the first campsite, I told Naomi and Johan that I was grateful we were hiking together.

We didn’t talk a lot while actively moving and all agreed during another break that the silence was a relief during such intense cardiovascular activity.

All of us were very similar and got along really well. I was relieved each time they elected to take a break for snacks and rest, laughing when they mentioned I could go on if I didn’t want to stop.

This section of the trail carves through a valley of tall, jagged rock faces and even though this first day would be the easiest, I felt every second pass by extremely slowly because of the heavy pack on my back.

When the clouds started to roll in and rain began to fall, we found shelter just outside the campsite and Johan made tea for everyone.

Of course my rented backpack didn’t come with a rain cover and I couldn’t easily access my rain coat so my sleeping mat got a bit wet.

Once the rain stopped we only had 10 more minutes to go before reaching the first campsite. I had tried to keep my phone off to conserve its power for the remainder of the trek and was happy Johan was leading the navigation.

The trail was easy to follow in any case but it was hard to refrain from taking photos or videos of the beauty around us.

The campsite isn’t like those you see in North American national parks. There aren’t picnic tables or any kind of bathroom facilities but there is a rushing river for water and vibrant green plots of land divided by rocky walls and broken boulders. Scattered upon most of the land where people sleep was a lot of cow, horse and donkey poop, not to mention human feces, toilet paper and litter everywhere you look.

What surprised me most was the small general store run by a mountain rescue worker who also sold beer, snacks, cigarettes and access to power for device charging.

Naomi, Johan and I set up our tents quickly in the light rain and took shelter inside them until it stopped. I was invited to drink beer with them, the rescue worker and a man with donkeys not too long later.

Each of us took turns buying beer for the group and got to know each other more while I practiced my Spanish with them. We danced, enjoyed the sunset and I learned the man with donkeys would be available tomorrow to carry my gear for 70–100 soles.

The beer kept flowing, we all kept dancing and pulled in another man with a horse passing by to join us whose birthday it was! No one was paying anymore.

As the only single woman amongst us, there was flirtatious talk aimed at me from both Esteban the donkey controller and the rescue worker whose name I sadly didn’t hear well enough to recall. We danced together, took selfies, shared hugs and I accepted kisses on my hand and cheek.

Of course my understanding was that all of the talk was good, joking fun but that didn’t stop Esteban from whispering my name outside the tent after I had gone to sleep. I pretended not to hear him and he didn’t persist further but I knew Naomi would have my back to ward him off with her perfect Spanish if need be.

The three of us made dinner as the stars came out and I finished the last of my tiny cup of beer while waiting for the water to boil for my Irish Shepherd’s Pie MRE.

We thought the alcohol would help us all sleep well that evening but I could still hear the incessant barking of the young wild dog that followed us in from the trailhead who had been running rampant around the campsite chasing things far and wide until early in the morning.

At some point in the night I got up to find a private place to have my first poop of the day far away from our tents. I squatted for quite some time before my body understood what it needed to do. Once the solid mass was out of me, a more liquid movement came out right after. That was strange but it felt good not to be constipated from the early morning.

Once I wiped and stood up, I made the mistake of looking at what I’d just done with my headlamp and immediately heaved over, vomiting up every bite of the dinner I consumed just hours before. Dammit.

The vomit kept coming. It was chunky and hard to extract from my throat. I was disgusted and relieved once it was done but worried for my energy levels for the next day now that nothing was inside of me anymore.

I went back to sleep until the sun began shining on our tents and I could hear Naomi and Johan beginning to pack up.

From inside my tent and before I could even make it outside, I puked again. This time it was just a bit of liquid bile but I knew I was in no state to regain strength through eating for the day’s hike to the next campsite.

But after brushing my teeth and releasing liquid through my asshole, I slowly packed up and got myself ready to hike. The sun felt so strong even with my hat and after applying sunscreen. I was short of breath and moving really slowly.

Naomi told me that Esteban had lost his donkey overnight and wouldn’t be able to carry my gear. Knowing the trail was about to get steep and that the next camp was significantly higher in altitude, I ultimately decided I couldn’t continue on in my current state.

I was low on toilet paper so asked Naomi and Johan if they could leave me with some before they left the campsite and they graciously did.

I thought I could walk out that morning the same way we’d hiked in together but after taking almost an hour to eat one apple, I knew I wouldn’t make it in time for the transportation back to Huaraz.

The rescue worker suggested I stay another night at the same camp to recover so I set my tent back up to rest in privacy.

The sun was hot on my tent but I kept the doors open to feel the constant breeze and it didn’t rain. At one point I puked up the apple outside my tent and had to pull out the pegs to move it to another location, away from my vomit.

I lay almost naked for the entire day, pooping liquid every few hours. I remembered the antibiotics I brought so I took my first round of them which seemed to help with the diarrhea.

By sunset, the rescue worker came to check on me and brought me tea to help with my nausea. It tasted slightly like anise and was black but delicious.

I mustered up enough strength to buy a Gatorade for dinner from his store and cried when I saw the blue kind. I gave him a hug and asked about what would happen if I didn’t feel better the next day. He seemed pretty certain I’d be okay but if worse came to worse I could take a helicopter straight back to Huaraz. There was also an emergency horse.

Back in my tent, I slept very well throughout the night, especially without the barking dog who thankfully followed a couple back out earlier in the morning. There was one other tent at the campsite that night but I didn’t talk to the people in it.

When dawn came, I felt much better and had plenty of energy to make oatmeal, eat some oranges and pack up my stuff.

I left most of my food and the garbage bag I’d been collecting with the rescue man from the store so my bag was significantly lighter for hiking out.

The trail was flat or downhill and I could see the couple who left before I did ahead of me for most of the hike out.

I loved being able to use my phone for photos and videos of all the stuff I wasn’t comfortable capturing on the way in.

I stopped at one point to poop and saw blood when I wiped but quickly realized I had just gotten my period. Thankfully I had a few small tampons but not a lot more toilet paper. Of course I bled through my underwear and shorts so I had to take those off and wash them in the river before finishing my hike out.

I had no idea how I was going to get back to Huaraz but I was prepared to ask for help finding a colectivo when I was done.

It was peaceful and enjoyable to walk the 9 km by myself with a bag I wasn’t thinking about the entire time now that it was a more manageable weight. I talked out loud to my mom after seeing some orange butterflies instead of listening to anything on my AirPods.

When I exited the trail, there was a car waiting with the hikers who were ahead of me and the driver whistled for acknowledgement that I needed a ride. I have no idea if the hikers told the driver I was on my way or if the driver insisted on waiting until the car was full before leaving but by some miracle I was whisked into the nearest town for 30 soles and didn’t ask anyone any questions.

After an hour of driving, we were back in Caraz and I was ushered into a colectivo van to get back to Huaraz. This time, my large hiking bag was put in the back of the van and I was able to sit in one of the 2 single seats.

I continued to struggle with other riders listening to their phones out loud without headphones and even said to one man “Por favor, mucho ruido” gesturing to my ears when he was standing over me watching a video.

There is no maintenance of personal space on this kind of transit but it was entertaining to watch people squish on with their various kinds of baggage, baskets and crates.

Back in Huaraz, I returned my gear a day early but didn’t get any money back. Thankfully the Airbnb I had reserved was able to accommodate me a day sooner than expected and I picked up my bag across town from where I had been staying before.

I was relieved to still be feeling well and was excited to try out another Airbnb claiming to be quiet.

I became fixated on garlic bread after seeing an appetizing sign with a photo of it on my way to the new Airbnb.

When I sat down in the restaurant and tried to order, I was told they were all out! Thankfully I found the same dish at another restaurant but it took three attempts at ordering using my broken Spanish and Google Translate to clarify what exactly I wanted. “Pan de ajo especial con queso y pimiento pero sin jabón”

I picked up some popsicles from a convenience store for dessert but didn’t realize the new place I was staying didn’t have a freezer so I had to eat them back to back.

At this new Airbnb I learned the trade-off for quiet is no windows with any kind of view. In addition to the front door that opens into the kitchen, there was a second door closing off the bedroom area which made for a peaceful, albeit dark rest area.

Over the next couple of days, I consumed a lot of free Red Bull TV and tea while recovering further from the bacterial infection I was likely experiencing from not having boiled my water enough while camping. Somehow I was able to do a load of laundry on the 4th floor where the views of the city and mountains were nice to see.

I had to decide whether or not to sign up for a guided expedition I had planned for the next 8 days called Huayhuash. It would be easier in terms of not having to carry heavy gear but after the latest AllTrails review mentioned dogs barking at some of the campsites, I couldn’t see how hiking peaks for 7 days in a row at 5,000 metres after not having a good night’s sleep and having to share a tent would be enjoyable.

I’m not doing these adventures to suffer or to push myself to any kind of limit, unlike everyone on Red Bull TV. So I rebooked the overnight bus ticket to Lima a week earlier than originally planned and found a quiet Airbnb inside a San Isidro park with lots of natural light.

Either the popsicles, tea water or my filter bottle were a mistake because I continued to have diarrhea and to feel unwell while spending countless hours catching up on my shows: NCIS, CIA, FBI, Elsbeth, Cupertino, MasterChef Canada, Private Eyes, Survivor, Eternally Yours and Anna Pigeon.

The day of the night bus departure I had consumed two meals from the California Cafe that gave me confidence for the journey. I was looking forward to being lulled into sleep on my reclined seat at the top back of the double-decker bus.

I felt what I thought was anxiety before leaving my Airbnb but now I’m thinking it was the bacterial illness I continued to have because of my poor water-related choices.
