The couple from the hike, Naomi and Johan, were taking the exact same bus but were sitting on the first level so I briefly ran into them while we were boarding. The 30-minute walk to the station felt good but I started to feel uneasy again once I arrived at the terminal. I took some natural anti-nausea medication before stepping onto the bus and put on my pressure point wristbands that are known to help with transit sickness.

The first couple of hours were okay. I listened to podcasts until the man in front of me stopped talking on his phone. I typed out a message to show him that was asking how long he planned to be on the phone because I found the chatter after 10 PM extremely annoying but thankfully after an hour he hung up and I didn’t have to ask.

After one typical visit to the bathroom that was beside my seat for a pee, I went back an hour or so later when it felt like I was in a washing machine that wouldn’t let up and I certainly had to vomit.

In the small bathroom, I squatted down and started puking what tasted like tomato despite not eating anything tomato related into the toilet, flushing after each release so I didn’t have to look at it.

There was a small open window at least to help with the smell.

I started to fart as well and became nervous that I’d shit my pants at the same time so I sat on the toilet seat and puked into the urinal in front of me while starting the all-too-familiar pissing through my asshole experience at the same time.

You could also flush the urinal but it didn’t drain quickly and wasn’t as deep as the toilet so the bus turbulence tossed much of it onto the small surface area making up the floor. I tried not to step in the mix of water and vomit while continuing to expel everything from my body.

It felt like I was in the bathroom for hours trying to brace myself on the two handles from being tossed around.

I started to lose feeling in my limbs when sitting so I knew I had to stand up. I stuck one hand at a time out the open window and looked around for any kind of help button. There wasn’t one.

I couldn’t leave the bathroom just yet so I sat back down on the toilet and opened the door, yelling “por favor, necesito ayuda” over and over again until someone woke up to look behind themselves at me. I closed the door once we made eye contact hoping someone would come offer support but that didn’t happen.

I had to get off the bus. This was hell. There was no stopping at a light and no long stretch of smooth highway to recover on.

When no one was coming to help me in the bathroom and I was done using it, I took the garbage bag from the bin back to my seat and continued to puke while there.

Thankful that I didn’t cause any bad blood with the person in front of me earlier because of his long phone call plan, I grabbed his shoulder to wake him up and ask for help again in between my latest round of puking.

He understood I needed help and woke up the lady beside him so he could go downstairs to get the driver.

About 30 minutes later the driver pulled into a gas station and came up to assess me. He brought plastic bags for me to puke in and helped me take deep, long breaths in through my nose and out through my mouth of the fresh air from the open window in the bathroom.

I tried to tell him I wanted to get off and if it would be possible for me to call a car for the rest of the way to Lima but that didn’t happen and likely wouldn’t have been safe.

The stopped bus was a nice break for my system and I took a Gravol with the assistance of his phone light. There couldn’t possibly be anymore in me to puke up, right?

Wrong. Not two hours later did I awake from a light nap to puke liquid loudly into one of the small white bags the driver had given me earlier. I could tell that was the Gravol coming back up.

A man a couple rows ahead of me sprang up to help, offering me an antibiotic pill, his bottled water and telling me he has gone through this before. It was likely a bacterial infection from the tap water I continued to drink through my filter bottle that obviously wasn’t reliable.

I learned he was from Florida but lives in Peru now and I thanked him excessively. He told me he lives near the airport with his wife in case I needed further help and he gave me his business card.

A little while later the bus had stopped. I was delusional and confused because only the Good Samaritan from Florida got off and I couldn’t move fast enough to gather my things and follow him. I had thought the bus only made one stop but I guess there were two.

I couldn’t open my map to see where we were or where the bus was headed for fear of becoming sick again but I was disappointed to have missed my chance to get off immediately and nervous about where I was going to end up.

Turns out we were heading deeper into the city which was closer to where I had booked to stay so that was okay. When the bus was parked, I hurried off and out of the busy terminal to a bench in the fresh air where I could privately burst into tears from such an overwhelming, horrible experience.

Once I had settled down, I called a Didi car and elected to pay cash upon arrival at my Airbnb. Of course the driver did not have the change required for me to pay so I ended up asking the handful of strangers around the park where I was staying while the driver waited.

No one seemed able to help but I think it was because certain bills here are more likely to be counterfeit. So I took the driver’s phone number and said I could transfer him the money instead. Realistically that was not going to be easily possible.

A park security guard tried to call for help so I could pay the driver but he had left before her contact made it to me. A man with a bike who originally said he did not have change ended up being able to provide enough that I could pay the driver so I messaged him a photo of the cash and asked him to come back for it while I waited.

Of course I had to pee and it took around 20 minutes for the driver to return but I tipped well and was glad to be free of that debt, thanking everyone around me as well.

After some access code confusion, I made it into my San Isidro Airbnb, situated inside a gated park and started the next chapter of my trip amongst a bunch of ants.

Feelings check

With the amount of crying, puking and shitting, I was obviously a shell of myself during this entire experience.

I was disappointed that I couldn’t complete the Santa Cruz hike and lost the motivation to sign up for Huayhuash. But I am also proud that I continue to know when to quit and to not push myself beyond my limits.

I knew going into this trip that I’d become sick at some point and would likely have to alter some plans so technically all is going as expected.

After seeing some photos from the couple I had met of the Santa Cruz trek, it didn’t feel like I was missing much in terms of views.

I was also relieved not to be stuck in dirty clothes for the next 7 days straight and sharing a tent with someone I don’t know during a very hard trek. I’m sad to miss out on the opportunity for daily exercise in a beautiful place with little food but that comes from disordered eating and can’t be how I make decisions.

I felt good knowing once and for all that I do not love backpacking or holding heavy things on my back. I enjoy long day hikes and taking multiple rest days between them.

Becoming overstimulated on transit and in public is real for me and it’s worth it to consider private transportation or alternative experiences that cater to those needs.

I know I can get along well socially with others and people build lasting bonds when they spend multiple days together on an adventure but it’s not actually something I enjoy or can handle happening frequently.

If there isn’t solo, peaceful downtime then I probably can’t easily participate.

I had a lot of fun drinking and dancing at the campsite with Naomi, Johan, Esteban and the wonderful rescue worker but it takes a lot of masking to ward off unwanted advances and to hold boundaries in a friendly, socially acceptable way.

I loved hiking out by myself and getting the chance to talk to my mom and to feel close to her surrounded by the natural beauty of nature. I know she continues to be proud of me, no matter what I do or don’t do.

I love being active and moving my body in a gentle way for long hours but exertion where I can’t quiet my mind and take in my surroundings is not enjoyable.

I will have plenty of opportunities to conquer challenging day hikes throughout Patagonia and it’s okay that I’m not able to say that I did a multi day trek by myself.

on the trail

Trail review

Uncrowded, easy-to-follow trail with campsites covered in donkey, cow and horse shit

Cost

140 soles for transportation, 80 soles per day for gear rental, 60 soles park fee.

Length

9.2 km from Cashapampa trailhead to Llamacorral campsite (50+ km total).

Difficulty

Extremely hard if you’re not used to carrying all your own gear and food.

Views

River valley surrounded by tall rock walls, boulders and a snowy peak in the distance.

People

Hardly anyone on the trail during mid-October and only one other group camping.

Transportation

Colectivo from Huaraz to Caraz and taxi from there to the trailhead.

Weather

Moderate temperatures and chilly overnight, strong sun, overcast, rain, wind.

Terrain

Sandy, rocky and grass-covered areas along a rushing river filled with animal poop.

Requirements

Water filter or ability to boil water, sun protection, camping gear and food.

Amenities

Store at camp with power, satellite service, snacks, drinks and cigarettes for sale.

where I stayed

Accommodation review

Dark and relatively quiet apartment perfect for rest and recovery after camping

Bed

Very comfortable queen-size bed with two pillows, soft sheets but smelly blanket.

Space

Small and functional with lots of built-in storage perfect for one person, but chilly.

Views

None from the apartment due to a frosted front window and no other windows.

Neighbourhood

Just on the outside of the main square located down a bit of a hill on a quiet street.

Noise

No outside noise with second door closed but can hear people from unit above.

Host-pitality

Co-hosts to answer questions promptly and to bring extra items like toilet paper.

Privacy

Unit is behind a gate on the 3rd floor without windows so is very private.

Value

Not bad if the oil and vinegar would have been full but more toilet paper was given.

Getting around

Food, pharmacies and more all within 5–30 minutes of enjoyable walking distance.

Cleanliness

Kitchen, bedroom and bathroom all spotlessly clean but blanket needed a wash.

Balanced reflections

Joy?
  • Preparing for a self sufficient solo hike
  • Meeting Naomi and Johan for hike support
  • Sharing drinks and dancing at the campsite
  • Hiking out alone feeling strong and healthy earlier than expected
  • Seeing a car waiting at the trailhead when I was finished
  • Flexible Airbnb hosts accommodating early check in and bag storage
  • Recovering in a near silent, dark low sensory room and doing laundry
  • Walking to the bus station at night with all my luggage
  • Help received on the overnight bus to Lima from the Florida man
Pain?
  • Feeling the weight of my fully loaded backpack for hiking
  • Overstimulation on the colectivo to and from the trailhead
  • Puking up dinner and everything else after not boiling water enough
  • Not having energy to continue hiking on the second day
  • The sound of dogs barking at night even at the remote campsite
  • Feeling unsettled after trusting my filter water bottle for the tap water
  • Being cold in the Airbnb and unwilling to leave the bed easily
  • Anxiety or the beginning of nausea at the bus station before boarding
  • Annoyance towards the man talking on his phone on the night bus
  • Being tossed around for 8 hours on the night bus, puking and shitting at the same time in the tiny bus bathroom without access to relief or help when needed

title: Alarm set for 4 AM
subtitle: Laguna 69
content:
My body breaks down over 4,500 metres

Waking up to an alarm unnaturally before dawn is something I usually avoid at all costs because it typically means my body hasn’t gotten enough sleep to function enjoyably the next day.

For a high altitude hike three hours away from where I was staying however, it was the only option.

It’s not too bad if you can drug yourself to sleep by 8 PM and have a bag prepared for the next day but being on a bus full of people making any kind of noise whatsoever felt overstimulating.

I understand that it’s normal to use your phone without headphones and to take calls in otherwise silent environments here. I couldn’t help but glare every time someone was engaging in such behaviour, especially before any light entered the sky.

At least I wasn’t nauseous.

I organized my transportation through the Mont Blanc travel agency which was just outside of the main plaza in Huaraz. You can also book a fully guided experience but I wanted to hike at my own pace.

The bus stopped for everyone to get breakfast after a chilly sunrise. I used the washroom before eating a banana and the jam croissant I packed. The restaurant offered a variety of breads, spreads, eggs, avocado and fruit juice, coffee or tea. Most people ate something and a few ordered sandwiches to go for the hike later. Processed snacks and drinks were also available for purchase in case you didn’t have enough water, for example.

At the trailhead, there were outhouses for use at 1 sol but I missed the sign and accidentally used one without paying, using my own toilet paper.

Nervous I wasn’t going to make it back to the bus in time, I started briskly on the deceivingly flat trail that was still taking my breath away with its slight incline starting at 3,900 metres.

Cows were grazing by the river and I appreciated the signs prohibiting noise although that didn’t seem to faze at least one couple listening to music out loud from a phone.

I worked my way around most groups so as not to be disturbed by anyone else’s presence or pace while stopping to take photos and video at my leisure.

Once the first set of switchbacks started, I stopped for a snack break to marvel at the waterfall behind me. The glaciated peak in the distance was unlike anything I’ve seen before.

Climbing further up passing donkeys and huge rock walls with signs that Laguna 69 was getting closer and closer was easier than I expected.

There was a smaller lake about an hour away that hikers hung out at on their way back down and it was surrounded by glacier views.

I was relieved the trail flattened out for the next while into a valley following the lake before ascending steeply into switchbacks again.

After applying SPF 100 sunscreen for the third time and starting to look like a ghost, I started slowly up the final part of the trail.

You know how on Everest people move comically slow near the peak? That is how it felt climbing to Laguna 69. Some people were so close and had to take extended breaks near the top, thinking they wouldn’t be able to make it because of altitude sickness.

But of course, one slow step at a time and with a lot of heavy breathing, I made it as an earlier group was starting their hike down.

Several people told me I was close and to keep going as we shared the trail. I would have preferred to finish the ascent with no one around detracting from the beauty but it was beautiful in any case.

At the top, I immediately tried to find coverage from the sun to eat my delicious avocado, tomato and queso fresco sandwich.

Couples were sprawled out around the rocky lake resting and enjoying the sun.

After eating, I asked the woman who sat beside me on the bus to take some photos of me and I reciprocated by snapping more of her and her boyfriend.

Our liaison was prompt to tell us when to start heading back in order to make the bus. As long as I remained ahead of him, I was sure to make my original transportation plan back into Huaraz.

I started to rush ahead of people from the bus who were stopping to take photos to ensure I’d get the same seat. I was worried the couple sitting separately would aim to ride back beside one another and I couldn’t be saddled with a new seat buddy in a different area of the bus.

Despite the trail being an out-and-back, turning around offered equally fantastic views of glaciers, tall rock walls and waterfalls.

I stopped several times when no one was around to take in deep breaths of silence before going back to the city noise.

I found out the porta-potty at the trailhead was only accessible with money when I tried to use it on my way out and was accosted by an employee. I did have soles to pay but my annoyance urged me to find a better spot to squat off a trail outside of the entrance.

After eating the rest of my snacks and taking anti-nausea medication, I boarded the bus and listened to my latest audio book about autism on the three hour drive home.

I was lucky the bus was rolling right past my place outside of the city so I asked to be dropped earlier instead of sitting in traffic while having to pee.

After a nice hot shower and a late night snack, I got to sleep as early as possible before the morning construction noise, roosters and barking dogs.

Feelings check

During the bus ride back to Huaraz, my left knee was in pain and needed space to straighten out. I enjoyed running down the steepest parts of the trail because I usually don’t hike with poles but perhaps the light impact isn’t the best on my aging joints!

The last 100 metres of Laguna 69 were wildly hard despite the spectacular views. My cardiovascular exhaustion while carrying only a day bag was cause for concern when considering multiday treks at even higher altitudes for next week.

I’m impressed that I was able to get up at 4 AM for pickup and that I spent more than 12 hours outside of where I was staying. I can do most things after a full 8 hours of sleep, it seems :)

The bus full of hikers was overstimulating as anticipated and I was bothered by trying not to rub arms with the woman who sat next to me but there were only a couple other buses at the trailhead, making the entire trail mostly absent of people.

Knowing what to expect, I would consider hiking this trail again.

on the trail

Trail review

Stunning glacial out-and-back trail with a slow and almost impossible final ascent

Cost

60 soles (~$25 CAD) for shared bus transportation to and from the trailhead plus 30 soles to enter the park.

Length

14 km going from 3,900 m to 4,600 m as an out-and-back starting off flat then transitioning to switchbacks.

Difficulty

Begins easy enough on a flat trail before moderately challenging switchbacks into a level valley before a very hard final ascent.

Views

Moraines, waterfalls & glaciated peaks in all directions: Chacraraju, Pisco, Yanapaccha, Huascarán, Chopicalqui & Huandoy.

People

Only a few bus loads of people for the entire day offering many opportunities for hiking with no one around.

Transportation

Hired private shared transportation through Mont Blanc tour agency but heard you could also take colectivos.

Weather

No rain despite the forecast predictions, windy at the top by the lake and an overall clear, sunny, warm and dry day.

Terrain

Starts off on a paved trail before ascending onto compact sandy switchbacks into a rocky flat path with one small river crossing.

Requirements

Strong sun protection, water and change for the porta-potty. Food for the trail and to sustain the 6 hours of travel time.

Amenities

Snack and drink are available at the trailhead with porta-potties for pay and seemingly donkeys for hire.

Balanced reflections

Joy?
  • The incredible views of nature and peace of experiencing it mostly solo
  • Not experiencing nausea on the bus
  • Hiking fast enough to make it back for my return transportation
Pain?
  • Fury towards anyone who reclined their seat on the bus, especially on the way back when I needed space for my knee to recover
  • Shortness of breath and sun violence during the final 100 m

title: Ubering to the trailhead
subtitle: Laguna Churup
content:
The higher costs of a lower sensory experience

If you’re staying in the centre of Huaraz then catching transit to the Laguna Churup trailhead makes a lot of sense. It’s affordable and allegedly comes frequently.

I was about a 25-minute walk away and wasn’t confident about finding the correct stop or vehicle when having to start early. Knowing time was of the essence and also fearing crossing the somewhat vicious neighbourhood dogs at such an early hour, I scheduled an Uber to take me to the trailhead.

The 45-minute drive was affordable and the right decision for me before my first acclimation hike. It was worth it to avoid any group chatter or social experiences that would have drained my energy before the hike.

I was nervous about the altitude and how hard the trail would be for me, especially after one AllTrails review compared it to Vancouver’s Grouse Grind but at 4,500 metres.

When I arrived at the trailhead, I sat out front and ate my first few snacks for breakfast. The wild dogs kept me company and it was hard not to feed them.

A man approached me and I told him I’d need a ride back into town after estimating it would take me 7 hours to complete.

After finding a private place to squat and pee, I started up the stairs and paid another man the park entrance fee of 30 soles (~$12.50 CAD). You can get a 3-day pass for 60 soles too.

The first half of the hike was similar to the Grouse Grind only insofar as there were a lot of stairs. However, the stairs were not steep and you had incredible views of snowy mountains and jagged rock faces in full sunlight to keep you occupied. In Vancouver, the trail is covered in forest before reaching the view at the top of the trail.

I appreciated the several shelters placed strategically for snack and water breaks on the way to the top.

The trail was easy to follow and there weren’t a lot of people on the hike so it often felt like I had it all to myself! The hardest part was the sustained stairs that made up the beginning but then it flattened out briefly.

There is a loop to the lake and you can choose to continue upwards if you love torture or you can keep on the flat direction for a bit of a break. There is no surprise which direction I picked.

Continuing to the right, there was a campsite near a waterfall where I stopped for more snacks to maximize my energy for the chain assisted climb to the lake.

I could see people scrambling at the top and couldn’t wait for the hike to become hands on. The dynamic nature of the hike was impressive and kept me very engaged. I agree with other AllTrails reviewers that it’s much easier and more enjoyable to use the chains for climbing up than it would be for going back down.

Once at the top, I lost the trail momentarily over some boulders and almost led some other hikers astray but was elated when I saw the glacial water shortly after.

Laguna Churup and the peak above it, Nevado Churup, are stunning. There were many places to sit and eat lunch. One couple was kind enough to offer to take a photo of me after seeing my attempt at a selfie.

There was another trail to a second lake and I appreciated that you could explore further. I found another private place to pee before rounding out the loop back to the trailhead in hopes there would be transportation waiting.

Going down is always a relief from the ascent but not without anxiety of slipping or sore knees. I don’t regularly hike with poles yet but I assume that would help.

So I continued to take breaks for water and snacks, relishing in the silence of the beautiful place I was in. I saw a few orange butterflies on the way up and felt the presence of my mom cheering me on.

The 6 km hike took me just about 6 hours to complete and I was nowhere near as out of breath as I was during the Ajusco peak circuit outside of Mexico City. I’m sure that had to do with the altitude pills I started taking and being better fed this time around.

After the descent there were two vans waiting for hikers to take them back into Huaraz. I think I paid 20 soles for the return trip. For comparison, scheduling the Uber back would have been slightly more than double that.

The only downside is the van waits until it’s full of passengers before leaving. I liked that there were a couple solo seats so I didn’t have to sit awkwardly beside someone.

Most of us chatted with one another about other trails in the area, sharing recommendations. I told everyone about the personal-item-sized bag I was travelling with for 5 months and they were all impressed :)

I made sure to take anti-nausea medication before the van took off and was pretty sleepy by the time I got home. After showering, I was in bed by 7 PM and delighted to drift into sleep after drowning out the noise of barking dogs with sleep music and ear plugs.

Feelings check

Wildly proud that I had a full day outside of the home in nature doing what I love in a safe and prepared way. As well as:

  • happy I didn’t overwhelm myself with catching transit and a short walk to the city centre in the morning so I could have extra sleep
  • good that I packed water with electrolytes for added energy
  • excited that I unlocked a new trail food — leftover chicken fried rice (arroz chaufa) which was delicious for lunch at the lake and didn’t need warming up
  • grateful for the moments of peace and being away from the noise of society
  • in slight disbelief that I coordinated the logistics to make this solo hike happen and nervous anticipation for the others to come

It feels reassuring to be one hike closer to getting back to the outdoorsy, adventurous and active person I am and want to continue being.

on the trail

Trail review

Dynamic ridge trail with consistently beautiful views that starts harder than it ends

Cost

30 soles to enter the park & 30 soles to Uber (cheapest with a colectivo) + cost of snacks / lunch = ~$25–30 CAD.

Length

7 km going from 3,850 m to 4,450 m as an out-and-back with loop to lake included and option for extension to second lake.

Difficulty

Starts off hard with stairs to climb initial elevation but includes many places at the beginning to take a break.

Views

Incredible views from every direction filled with glaciated peaks, boulders and, of course, the stunning emerald lake.

People

Just enough to feel like I was in the right place but not enough where it felt like I was sharing the trail for long periods of time.

Transportation

Colectivos wait at the trailhead to take hikers back to the city but they don’t leave until each seat is full and paid for.

Weather

Sunny morning with little cloud coverage, wind or shade offered but rain came later in the afternoon for the ride home.

Terrain

Easy-to-follow sandy and compact gravel trail with periods of dynamic boulder scrambling assisted by chains.

Requirements

Food, sun protection, water and shoes with good grip at the minimum. Consider poles for the descent or running down.

Amenities

Snacks and beverages sold in the afternoon at the trailhead. Shelters for the first couple of kilometres. Toilet after the initial stairs.

Balanced reflections

Joy?
  • The private Uber pickup for reduced sensory overload and more sleep
  • Glaciated and raw mountain views from every direction
  • The silence of nature and from other hikers for several kms
  • Enjoying chicken fried rice in front of the stunning lake
  • Chains used to climb the steep, boulder sections
  • Relatively flat ascent to the lake after a sustained start of stairs
Pain?
  • Fear for my first official high altitude hike of this trip in Peru and whether or not I’d be able to do it within the 6-7 hours the trail was open with return transportation that wasn’t certain
  • Starting the altitude climb up exposed stairs and breaking in my cardiovascular system after a while of low activity

title: Roosters, dogs and construction
subtitle: Plus a really friendly Airbnb host
content:
Inescapable noise pollution is sickening

Only 7 more minutes until construction is required to stop for the day. The roosters and dogs don’t make noise on a schedule but at least they’re less deafening.

My Airbnb in Huaraz, Peru was primarily described as quiet but unfortunately even after midnight, the atmosphere is anything but peaceful.

I recognize that:

  • construction is advantageous for an increase in livelihood,
  • roosters provide food for families,
  • dogs alert the neighbourhood for protection and
  • my main travel value is to live locally but

I’m finding it very challenging to hear my own thoughts.

It’s now 2 minutes after construction is supposed to cease and I can still hear metal scraping in what feels like the room beside where I write this.

My host Miguel told me the construction is ongoing for 20 days. I 100% would have found another place if I had known.

I keep telling myself that this state will not be forever and soon I will only know the lonely silence of nature but it’s hard not to cut my stay here short to try another place.

The first 24 hours

When I arrived in Huaraz I was blown away by the mountainous landscape towering over the sprawling city. Every direction you look there is a snowy peak to marvel at.

The Airbnb I chose was newer, with only 20 reviews but a 5-star rating. There was no house manual or recommendation guide for the neighbourhood so I had a lot of questions for the host Miguel.

When home from work, Miguel took me into the city to buy potable water and house shoes. It was nice to explore with a local and I appreciated his willingness to make my stay comfortable.

When we were standing in line to pay for the shoes, he asked if we could take a photo together. I was alarmed by the request, fearing I was about to be trafficked because he had just gotten off the phone with someone so I said no and offered my new Instagram account instead.

The next morning he took me into town again and we visited 4 different tourist excursion places so I could plan my various treks while here. He helped me communicate with each tour operator and we found one place offering everything I was looking for at affordable prices.

Later, he assisted me with doing laundry and BeReal went off so I asked him if we could take a photo for the memory, likely feeling badly I had denied his request from the day before.

We made plans to hang out later that evening but I bailed to work on this blog. He mentioned having some wine together and possibly going dancing.

Am I wrong to suspect he might be romantically interested in me?

We spoke about both being divorced and he mentioned having two kids. I saw where he worked and have not been shy about telling him I struggle with the noise each time he checks in.

I realize I don’t really have the clothing or footwear to go out dancing and that agreeing is likely leading him on but a night out with a local would be fun so I’m open to the experience should I have the energy after my acclimation hikes.

Feelings check

I was equally excited and nervous to explore the city on my own to procure groceries. Miguel told me about a new grocery store nearby and I noticed endless places to eat in the neighbourhood.

I was surprised to notice no fresh produce, cheese or bread in the massive store that was also empty of shoppers. If the locals aren’t shopping there then I probably shouldn’t be either!

I didn’t realize I was a 20-minute walk from the centre of the city, which is filled with produce stands and local markets.

I still feel uncomfortable walking around unaccompanied, which is a feeling I haven’t had on prior trips. I’m very aware about whether or not I am crossing the street correctly, if I’m walking in the right areas or if I’m saying the right words when ordering food.

The anticipation of being perceived is causing me to stay inside more than usual when travelling and being in my accommodation with all the noise and less natural light than I am used to is starting to feel strange.

I know this is just a lengthy transition period and that by the end of this 5 months away from home I will likely feel much different but for now, it feels notable.

where I stayed

Accommodation review

Large apartment with helpful host surrounded by construction, dogs and roosters

Bed

Cozy bed with a variety of blankets and two pillows providing ideal warmth at night.

Space

Large second-floor apartment with lots of windows and natural light in the bedroom.

Views

Local residential street with hills and mountains in the distance from bedroom.

Neighbourhood

20-minute walk from city centre but plenty of places to get food or eat nearby.

Noise

Deafening construction next door with dogs and roosters going off at all hours.

Host-pitality

Very friendly and helpful by taking me into town for tour information, water and shoes.

Privacy

Tinted windows and frosted glass with curtains and hook provide privacy indoors.

Value

I appreciated the blender, variety of tea, rice, spices, cookware and oil provided.

Getting around

Necessities all within walking distance with affordable Ubers and taxis always available.

Cleanliness

Photos looked better than reality. Needs a deep clean but livable and not many bugs.

Balanced reflections

Joy?
  • Practicing Spanish with Miguel
  • Catching up on Netflix in two rooms
  • The affordable market food
  • Stunning city and mountain views from the upper-floor laundry area
Pain?
  • The lack of natural light in the main room is limiting to motivation
  • The construction between 8:30 AM–5:30 PM Monday to Saturday makes it hard to create content, not to mention the roosters and dogs

title: When a stranger goes in for a kiss
subtitle: The “no gracias” hat isn’t working
content:
Travelling: 100% guaranteed to meet people

Despite my best efforts to appear unapproachable, it’s impossible not to make new connections in every city I visit.

This time, on the streets of Barranco in Lima, Peru after one hour biking along the coastal cliffs, a younger-looking man stopped me to ask about the brand of my Nalgene filter water bottle.

His name is Claudio.

After snapping a photo of the bottle, we walked together up some stairs surrounded by bright, gorgeous mural art to a lookout I wouldn’t have known to visit without his local knowledge.

I spoke with him in my broken Spanish and he knew a bit of English so we got to know a few facts about each other.

  • Claudio was on a break from work — a new job he doesn’t really enjoy
  • He likes hiking and has summited mountains but feels he’s a bit fat currently
  • When I asked him how old he was, he responded “old enough for you”

I shared my age, told him I didn’t want kids and talked about the trip I had planned.

I was nervous when he asked if I wanted a photo because I couldn’t risk having my phone stolen so I made up some excuse about only travelling with comfortable, functional and athletic clothing that didn’t warrant photographing.

It wasn’t long before he tried to put his arm around my waist and to hold my hand.

Now that I’m no longer a 20-something people-pleasing person desperate for attention, it was easy to firmly but politely ward off his advances.

We exchanged numbers and he invited me out after work that same evening but I declined based on my early flight the next morning.

So he double-kissed my cheeks goodbye and didn’t miss the opportunity to go in for my lips.

Again I pulled away and said we weren’t doing that. He understood and didn’t persist further.

It’s great to meet and learn from locals but what is with the rapid escalation to intimacy?

We’re texting a little and maybe I’ll have the chance to see him again before moving to the next country but I also don’t want to lead him on.

I’m barely looking for friends let alone something romantic!

Feelings check

I continued to experience anxiety leaving my accommodation without another person. I’m not exactly sure why… I think it’s because of the social norms required to function or blend in.

The energy required to secure a bike rental, order food or ask for information feels exhausting. I think that’s why I’m so obsessed with ordering food straight to where I am staying.

Maybe it’s just a longer transition and I’ll be feeling like more of my old self before the 5 months are up, but maybe this is also just who I am now.

You wouldn’t know outwardly that anything was wrong but I’m constantly hoping that with my large sunnies, hair pulled back, modest dress and hat that everyone will ignore my existence so I can enjoy my exploration solo.

I know social connection is important for overall happiness and I really do enjoy meeting new people, learning about them and experiencing new things together but the toll it takes on my energy levels is significant.

where I stayed

Accommodation review

Cute, cozy, clean and centrally located apartment that’s quiet when the windows are closed

Bed

Firm mattress, scratchy sheets and two of the same memory foam pillows.

Space

Small studio apartment with functional and clean kitchenette and large shower.

Views

Atlantic City casino, construction projects and a busy street with lots of activity.

Neighbourhood

Centrally located in busy area close to anything you need within walking distance.

Noise

With windows open, lots of honking and chatter but silent when they are closed.

Host-pitality

Didn’t meet but was provided with a helpful guide with recommendations.

Privacy

Even with the curtains open, the 6th floor provides lots of privacy.

Value

A couple of snacks were provided and were greatly appreciated after a red-eye flight.

Getting around

All necessities in walking distance and Ubers are affordable to get to the airport.

Cleanliness

Every corner was spotless but there was a bit of a damp water smell under the sink.

Balanced reflections

Joy?
  • Affordable Japanese-Peruvian food delivered by Rappi was delicious
  • Endless coastal and cliff side trail for biking, running and walking with gorgeous parks, arts and markets
Pain?
  • Mildly annoying to say no to a stranger’s advances multiple times
  • Daniel not making time to catch up on my polos after saying he’d be in touch with daily updates

title: When the best laid plans fail
subtitle: And it’s okay to turn back!
content:
How [not] to prepare for 5 months of hiking

  1. Stay home
  2. Lounge in the sun
  3. Smoke weed
  4. Eat chocolate
  5. Snuggle your cat (or dog, pillow, spouse)

Usually one may consider hitting the gym, regularly running or doing practice hikes at high altitude but I wanted to counteract the active lifestyle I was about to have with an opposite one filled with comfort and mostly sedentary activities.

I was pretty certain becoming active again would be like riding a bike. Of course a lack of appetite without marijuana and high altitude would slow me down but in time, I can do anything! Right?

So on my last day in Mexico City, I scheduled three Ubers to make one volcanic hike happen.

  • The first car would pick me up early in the morning to take me 1 hour to the Ajusco Peak trailhead.
  • The second would come when the hike was over, taking me back to my accommodation.
  • The third would bring me to the airport once I clean up and repack.

I gave myself 7.5 hours to do a hard 6 km loop before flying to Peru at 10 PM that same evening.

The blisters I sustained from walking over 25,000 steps in the city two days prior were bandaged. I even had snacks and cash for the park.

I felt well prepared, even double-checking the location of the restaurant I was using for the Uber drop-off and pick-up after learning there were two on opposite sides of the city.

So, with the help of a natural sleep aid, it was early to bed before catching the first car.

When I got out of the Uber on what seemed to be the side of a major motorway, I sat in Cabana Vicky’s about to order food when I noticed AllTrails said I was an 11-hour walk away…

What?

Sorry, WHAT???

How?

I put in the wrong Cabana Vicky’s… There are two, maybe more.

Feeling the clock ticking down, I ordered another Uber to take me to the correct location immediately and ate a packed snack in the shade while waiting.

It would be another 60-minute drive to where I wanted to go, meaning now I’d only have 6 or so hours to complete the hike before my flight.

I can still do this.

The Mexico City traffic was in full force now and the roads near the end were so steep I didn’t think the manual car would make it up. Cellular service was minimal and following any map app became unreliable. I have to think that is why the driver stopped and let me out somewhere that was still an 18-minute drive away from where I wanted to be.

So I ordered a third Uber to take me the rest of the way, slightly panicking about only now having 5 or so hours to complete the hike.

I was dropped off in the middle of nowhere, about a 5-minute walk away from the trailhead. There was a low wooden gate topped with barbed wire in front of a trail that I could see on my offline map connected to where I wanted to be.

So I hopped the fence and started my hike! I was pretty much gassed immediately because of the high altitude but assumed I’d adjust quickly.

The trail disappeared after a few minutes into overgrown brush so I was forced back onto the road, now covered in greenery and thankful for the immediate break from walking upwards.

Minutes later, I FINALLY ended up at the official front gate where you sign in and pay for the hike. Not many people were on the trail and no one was hiking solo.

I had barely started moving before having thoughts about turning around.

That is unlike me.

Plus the sunk cost of all those Ubers was weighing on me.

So with a carrot in hand to munch on for energy, I climbed.

Every 100 metres I must have stopped to catch my breath. I couldn’t even distract myself with music, podcasts, audiobooks or the beauty of nature. Breathing was so hard!

I could see from my map that it was only 3 km up before a leisurely walk down but after less than 1 km, I had to recalculate.

So I found a nice rock to enjoy the view from before turning back.

I reasoned that the higher I went, the foggier it would be so it’s not like I was going to get a better view from the top than what I had from where I was. I also wasn’t confident the Uber I scheduled to pick me up from that barbed wire fence would actually arrive given the lack of cellular service and I did not want to risk missing my flight or being rushed to repack.

A couple passed me on my break and we chatted briefly about where I was from and my plan to go back down.

I saw them later in the parking lot and they offered to take me into the nearest town where I’d have service to order an Uber to take me home.

Thank you Marco from Mexico and Daddi from Cuba!

I was grateful that the park employees also offered to drive me into cellular service and thought this must happen a lot to tourists.

Feelings check

Of course I felt a little silly for messing up the Uber drop-offs multiple times. I know I haven’t been eating enough so my mind and patience are not at their best. I was humbled by not being able to complete the hike and surprised at my lack of motivation to persevere. This experience worries me for my plans to complete future high altitude hikes.

I was extremely burnt out from all the car rides and couldn’t bring myself to go out for food after arriving back from the hike and before heading to the airport.

Napping felt natural but the dogs barking incessantly prevented that from happening for long.

On the bright side, the Popocatépetl volcano was very active before sunset and despite the noise keeping me awake, it was incredible to watch.

where I stayed

Accommodation review

The view was exceptional but all things considered, I probably wouldn’t stay again.

Bed

Cozy against the wall with the flannel sheets and a variety of 3 pillows.

Space

Small and functional with lots of big windows and bright yellow curtains.

Views

Incredible to see multiple volcanoes, the sprawling city and many Mexican flags.

Neighbourhood

Seemingly unknown by locals with lots of cute streets, mural art, stores and shops.

Noise

Loud with dogs barking, neighbours talking, people broadcasting and construction.

Host-pitality

Didn’t meet and no local advice was given but communication was reasonable.

Privacy

None on the balcony due to neighbours but lots if the curtains are closed.

Value

Not great given a lack of Wi-Fi out in the area and not enough tea or toilet paper.

Getting around

All necessities in walking distance and Ubers are affordable to get into the city.

Cleanliness

A few small bugs given there are no screens and stray hairs but otherwise clean.

Balanced reflections

Joy?
  • Affordable Ubers able to take me to random places so I never feel stranded
  • Watching volcanic activity from the privacy of my balcony
Pain?
  • Having shortness of breath while hiking at 3,500 metres
  • Not being well fed makes my temper short and my nervous system unable to deal with noise

title: Practico español
subtitle: Ordering food and drink
content:
After 930 days on Duolingo…

It’s finally time to use what Spanish I’ve learned online in the real world. The Uber driver didn’t have much to say on the way here but I’ve been chatting with my accommodation hosts and writing my daily journals en Español. Plus there is Netflix with Spanish subtitles.

I felt pretty confident ordering pollo enchiladas until they asked if I wanted a beverage and then brought me the largest michelada I’ve ever handled. After a few sips, I was tipsy and full. Thankfully you can take anything to-go in Mexico, even alcohol.

When I couldn’t pay, one of the employees offered to walk me to an ATM. That was a great opportunity to speak Spanish despite not being able to take out any cash. Luckily I was able to transfer him money for the meal. I asked him if he’d always lived here and he said yes but would like to visit Amsterdam. Of course then I had to ask him about marijuana and he told me he also likes LSD. I told him about the molly bears I brought and that this was the first day of my 5-month trip to practice Spanish in South America :)

During the quick walk back to my place, a family in a car stopped me to ask where I had gotten the takeout and beverage I was carrying. Unfortunately I was caught off guard and the traffic pressure did not allow me to respond helpfully.

Feelings check

I felt uneasy waking up in Mexico City for the first full day of 5 months away from home. I was nervous to leave my booking.com accommodation because of the masking required to interact even minimally with the public.

I know it’s obvious that I’m not from here and I need to be extra vigilant and safe with information I give out.

The neighbourhood where I’m staying is hilly, filled with graffiti murals and small shops that only accept cash. There are so many volcanic peaks dotting the landscape of the view from my apartment and a lot of trails to explore. It feels overwhelming not to be able to see the entire city and each national park in the less than 10 days I will be spending here.

It still doesn’t feel real that my adventure has begun. I’m not sure when that will change. I think starting with a low pressure rest day was smart. I wasn’t ready for a full day out walking so soon.

I’ll probably be hungover tomorrow!

Balanced reflections

Joy?
  • Daniel sending me polos and staying in touch via text, telling me he misses me, Hulky and him enjoying my balcony before the renter comes
  • Those first few sips of alcohol and talking to my Oma live at the restaurant I was eating at
Pain?
  • Physically my neck feels a bit stiff
  • Reminders of my time dating Jael and us meeting in Mexico. It doesn’t help that he’s messaging me, sending voice notes, calling me baby and trying to make plans to see me in February here

title: 5 months trekking through South America
subtitle: Solo travelling with a personal-item-sized bag
content:
With research and experimentation, you can pack less!

Almost every year I plan 3- or 4-month-long adventures to explore remote trails around the world and I’m taking off soon on my longest trip yet, 5 months!

When a carry-on sized item was included in most economy tickets, I’d take my favourite pastel roller bag onto the planes, a backpack and a pillowcase stuffed with extra clothing. Now that base fares only include a personal sized item, I’ll be taking just a small backpack, fanny pack and neck pillow case stuffed with smaller items.

What you decide to bring depends on where you’re going, the climate and weather, what you’ll be doing and your personal preferences. I’ve packed and repacked almost 20 times in the last 3 months, narrowing down my must-haves for trekking in South America — see the full pack list and rationale.

The benefits of travelling with JUST a personal-item-sized bag include:

  1. Avoiding airline baggage fees
  2. Saving time at the airport
  3. Zero lost bag anxiety
  4. Reducing daily decision fatigue
  5. Appearing less touristy

I went for a bag that would fit in the smallest of budget airline baggage sizers and that would hold its shape when fully loaded, the Sherpani Soleil. Light material like merino wool reduces the overall weight of the bag, as does holding heavier items like battery packs in a fanny pack or on your person in some other way. I try to avoid packing liquids for the same reason.

No matter what, the only shoes you can bring are the ones on your feet! I’m obsessed with Hoka’s Hopara line of all-purpose hiking shoes. They’re waterproof and I’ve run, walked endlessly and summited mountains in them.

All of this already feels like an accomplishment and I can’t wait to see if I’ve made all the right decisions or what I’d change for next time. Was every item packed used? Did the compression bag hold up? Was it possible to remain organized?

Feelings check

Only 10 days before I’ll be falling asleep in Mexico City, starting several adventures of a lifetime again. On the one hand, 5 months feels unfathomable. On the other hand, I know it’s going to fly by and I’ll be back to my vibrator and weed in no time. Coming back to essential oil diffusers, warm baths, Laneige lip masks and Aesop hand cream are experiences I will greatly anticipate upon return. Not to mention snuggling my cat again when she comes back for my birthday month and the opening of my balcony space with the sun’s return to it.

Life is good. I am lucky. This is so many dreams come true and my ideal lifestyle. I’m not employed but it’s a gift to be in this millennial pause or mid-career retirement, whatever you want to call it, while I have the good health and energy to see more of the beautiful world. I have to believe what’s meant to happen will and that I am making all the right moves to reveal my future opportunities.

From the written journal:
